div.p: At the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, before Councillor H Roberts fin the chair), end other magis- trates, a youth of seventeen. named James Alfred Silcock, 154, Forster-street, was charged on remand with having stolen a postal packet containing a fountain ren, on March 6th. Mr T S Steel defended. Mr H A Thew (Avison, Morton, Paxton and Co.) Liverpool, prosecuted and said that on the sth March a letter was made up by a lady in Liverpool and addressed to a gentleman in Warrington. It contained a fountain pen enclosed in a cardboard box. The letter was posted in the afternoon and would in the ordinary course have reached Warrington in the evening and been delivered by the accused on the following morn- ing. The package never reached its destination and in consequence an official Came down in July and questioned the accused on the matter. A search was made of his house where the cardboard box and the fountain pen were found. Prisoner then admitted he had raken it. The case was one which the bench could not deal with themselves. Mr Steel: He would have to be committed for trial -at the Liverpool Assizes. He bad been in communica- tion with the Postmaster-General and had placed certain circumstances before him and it had been arranged that be (Mr Steel) should apply to the bench -to reduce the charge so that it could be dealt with that morning. A document was handed to the magistrates and Mr Thew said he offered no opposition to the application in the circumstances. The charge was then reduced to the effect that Silcock stole a fountain pen, the property of Mr K Bolton, of Warrington-- Mr Thew : Or the Postmaster-General. Mr Steel : Yes. Mr Steel said that the defendant had admitted taking the pen and there were one or two facts he would like to point out to the bench. The youth had been in the employ of the Post Office for four ears. He started as a telegraph boy and was only just over 17 years of age. The taking of the fountain pen dated so far back as the 6th March and it was only when taxed by the detective from London that the defendant admitted the theft. Ile had spoken to the defendant who told him that be could not explain why he took the pen, and could only recount for his offence by sudden temptation. Fountain pens were an attraction to young people. There was no secrecy about him having taken the pen. He had told the detective where he could find it and as a matter of fact the defendant and his famity had used it. lie urged upon them the defendant's youthfulness. He was also the main support of his mother, brother and sister his father having died only recently. Mrs Silcock had a nephew in Australia and a passage for herself and family had been booked and they were due to sail in September. Ile asked that the defendant who wan about to start a fresh career in another country should not be branded as a gaol bird. He suggested that he should be bound over under the Probationers Act in view of his age and his previous good character. Mr Thew said there was one fact which had not been stated correctly by Mr Steel. On the boy being charged with the offence he did not admit it at first and it was only after the articles had been found in the house that be admitted they were the ones he had stolen. The original offence he was charged with was a very serious one and the maximum sentence was penal servitude for life. After some consideration the chairman said the bench were taking an extremely merciful view of the case in binding Silcock over to appear for judgment if called upon within twelve months, and to pay the costs amounting to 4s. Addressitg Silcock the Chairman said "You are starting an entirely fresh life and I hone, as do all my colleagues, that there will not be the slightest occasion in the future to bring this charge against you even by suggesti, n. Have respect for those for whom you work. You have a good opportunity which does liot often fall to people in your position. Borough Police Court. Mo&DAY.—Before Mr S Wright (in the chair), Alder- man James Evans, Councillor Wilkinson, Messrs W Roberts, W Furness, G Pilling, T Locker and Dr Fox. A PxutourcAr. WINDOW BREAM:R.—DanieI Crooks, forge labourer, Pinners Brow, was charged with having teen guilty of disorderly conduct and also with wilfully breaking a plate glass window t the Wheatsheaf Hotel, doing damage to the extent of £4.—Mr Steel, who prosecuted, on behalf of the Licensed Victuallers Ass )ciation, of which the landlord Mr Hughes is a member. said that at 6.10 pm. on Saturday. P.C. Summers was on duty in Orford-lane when he saw the prisoner go up to the building with a stone in his hand wilfully break the window. The officer went up to him and prisoner said "It's alright its only my—temper." With the assistance of Sergeant Woollacott he was brought to the Police Station. When charged he replied " I did it wilfully." Continuing, Mr Steel said it appeared to be a periodical attack made by prisoner on the house. That was the third time he had committed a similar offence. The landlord had refused to serve him for some time and when he had a drop of drink DOW he made straight for the house and did considerable , damage. He was a great nuisance. The Chief Con- stable said Crooks msde his 19th appearance. The damage was moat wantonly done. Crooks was sent to prison for two months with hard labour. A LONG LlST.—Anastatia, Crawley, of DO settled abode, made her 126th appearance on charges of having been drunk and disorderly and with having broken a , pane of glass in the police cell. She pleaded guilty.— The Chief Constable said that was the tenth charge of wilful damage against the prisoner, who had been con- victed 125 times previously, which was only part of her record. Vortunately she had given them a wide berth since January, 1911.—Crawley was sent to gaol for two months' hard labour.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Another of those capital programmes to which patrons of the Hippodrome ate accustomed is being presented this week and large houses are the rule. Excruciatingly funny are the antics of Palo and Selby in a comedy acrobatic scene "A clumsy acrobat." Within the limited area of a table top a number of successive summersalts are rapidly gone through and the attemps of the comedian to imitate his partner please and amuse the house immensely. A neat turn is given by Les Marco BAH, a couple of exceedingly smart entertainers. Some really clever sleight of hand tricks are well received but the audiences are surprised and nJt in the least mystified at the exposures so calmly and neatly given by the assistant. In a dramatic and humorous episode " Wrong los." Mr James Hares Company are fairly successful, five persons are involved and the sketch is full of exciting and humorous incidents. With a free style and possessing a good supply of smart gags the New Macs are at once favourites with the audience who welcome a return of this comical courOe who are real comedy merchants. Sam Kelly billed as a Scotch comedian—only Oiflereat—is indeed a clever artiste, his make-up and breezy style fully justifying his description on the bill. Riche and . Walker are smart wooden shoe dances and this part of , their turn makes up for the usual imitation coon- singing with which they begin their performance. In a simple little act the Sisters Royce and Sid show us what can be done in the way of simultaneous dancing and their performance is neat, skilful and palatable to the audience. Andie Barns is a good comedian and gives an acceptable blending of straight and ecceptric dancing in a pleasing manner. Fred Camplin also appears as a comedian. In addition, the usual fine pictures are shown on the bioscope.

The President of the Board of Trade hss received a notice from Major Dalrymple White of a question ask- ing whether his attention has been called to the rider ot a jury at Crewe, on July 22, at the inquest on Mrs James, who fell from a train through the opening of a carriage door, to the effect that some safety fastenings for railway carriage doors is urgently required, and whether in view of the numerous accidents that occur in this way he will take any steps that may be neces- sary to compel railway companies to adopt such fasten- ings.

div.head: LIBERAL ASSOCIATION'S CAMPAIGN,
div.p: LIBERAL ASSOCIATION'S CAMPAIGN,
Meeting at Catherine-street.

The open-air campaign of the Warrington Liberal Association proceeds apace and on Wednesday evening another good meeting was held in the vicinity of Catherine-street, Mr ft Osbo-ne, presided. The chief speaker was Mr Canning of Manchester, who reviewed the past work of the Liberal party for the people in a lucid manner, and spoke confidently of the future under a Liberal Government.

The CHAIRMAN briefly opened the meeting by referring to the Crewe election and said that the Coe- servative did not, although he was Member, repre- sent the mass of the people in that constituency. (Hear, bear.) He noticed from the papers that Mr. Lloyd George had made it possible for the children of insured persons under the Act to have the benefits of sanatoria as well as the great number of workers in the country who were suffering from consumption. (Applause). Mr. CANNING remarked on the tremendous inequali- ties of wealth and well-being which existed in the country. The function of any Government in .rt civilised country, worthy of the name, was that it should see to the well-being and comfort of all the people who were gathered under the national Brig. There were many questions which had to be dealt with for the general benefit, amongst which were the land and unemployment question. The people of this country did not starve or wei.as not unemployed when the land was not monopolised by wealthy people. Notwithstanding the general. pros- perity of the country, there was the "condition of Lugland "question which all the Governments bad to deal with in one way or another, if they did their duty to the people. (Hear, hear). There was not the slightest doubt about, the tremendous inequalities which existed at the present time. (Hear, hear). After quoting numerous figures to illustrate the unfair distri- bution of wealth the speaker said that one person in every seven was buried at the expense of the parish. The indirect taxation of the Tory Party meant that the greater share of the burden fell upon the man with the small income. (Hear, bear.) The policy of Tariff Reform the Tories were pushing for- ward, was one form of indirect taxation and the people who thought out those great questions for themselves would never for a moment entertain such a proposal. (Hear, hear). The Tories were making much ef.the Insurance Act at the present time and especially in Manchester. The Act affected the man's pocket directly but there were untold benefits which came for that, money and the people would find out in time that they could not, manage without the Act. (Hear, hear.) They could not possibly start any system of Insurance and begin drawing out before any money had been paid in. (Hear, hear.) Sickness, against which the Act provided Was responsible for one half of the pauperism of tee country. That was placing a burden on the poor-rate which the workingman had to pay in an indirect way and in time, when the Act was in proper working order, no doubt that rate would be reduced and thereby relieve the workers of a burden. (Applause). The Act would more to secure the well being of the people than any legislation he could remember. They were going to take care of all the people of the country in times of sickness and distress and they would very materially help to build up a stronger nation and a stronger race. (Applause.) In regard to Free Trade the people of Manchester would hear a great deal of that sensible policy within the next few days. On his way to the meeting he had passed a big wire works, lie did not know the name of it but there was a lot of black smoke issuing from the chimneys and the the inspector might have had his eye on it (Laughter). If the policy of Tariff Reform was adopted those works would probably have to practically close down and that would mean a swell on the unemployed market. (Hear, hear.) After illustrating the utter futility of erecting a ff wall in regard to the wire trade alone, Mr Canning dealt at some length with the land question and pointed out that in view of the feet that the people by their industry and skill had made the land values, those values ought to he taxed so that other burdens under which the great mass of workers in this eountry laboured might be made lighter The people must have the land to live upon and to maintain the industries in which they earned their living. (Hear, hear, They were perfectly entitled to tax the land values for the common needs of the people. (Hear, hear). The land owner did nothing to make his land more valuable, all that be did was to sit still and wait until the people wanted it and then he could get,a big price for it. (A voice : Shame.) It was the object of the Liberal Party to tax that land so that the people would benefit by having their too heavy burdens of indirect sod other taxation reduced. (Applause). Mr BROWN in proposing a comprehensive vote of thanks, said that al the people listened and learned their support of the present Government would increase. (hear, hear). Mr J BUTTON seconded and commended the "One man one vote " policy of the Liberal Party which would atop once and lor all the Plural Voting.(Applause)

div.head: PROGRESSIVE LABOUR LEAGUE.
div.p: PROGRESSIVE LABOUR LEAGUE.
BIG MEETING AT BRIDGE
Mr. A. H. Crosfield and Mr. Car

Special interest was taken in the open-air meeting held at Bridge Foot on Monday evening under the auspices of the Progressive Labour League, as the principal speakers were Mr A H Crosfield (who pre- sided) and Mr. Caradoc Rees, late Liberal candidate for the Denbigh boroughs. There was a large and enthusiastic crowd, and the cordial unanimity of the meeting was impressive, not a single dissentient voice being raised._ .

Mr. A. H. CrtosriELD, who bad a rousing reception, expressed satisfaction at seeing such a large and cheer- ful audience. They had had an untoward incident at Crewe which, of course, they regretted, but he thought their Tory friends who had such a lot to say about it in the Press were very easily pleased because, after all, if they took the total progressive vote at Crewe, they found a most satisfactory and substantial majority in favour of progress and Free Trade. (Applause.) It was particularly significant in view of the fact that when a Government had been in power a con- siderable time a wastage sometimes set in and what people usually called " the swing or the pendulum beou to operate. He saw very little sign of that in the country as yet. Tho reason was that education was telling its tale—(hear, bear)— and as our democracy got more and more educated it felt that the great and grave problems that went to the root of our national life were too serious to be trifled with in the way that some of their opponents trifled with politics to-day. (Applause.) The Crewe election afforded evidence that it was high _ _

TIME WE HAD THE ALTERNATIVE VOTE in English politics. (Hear, bear.) It was only right and fair that the Labour party, like the Liberal piny, should develop its influence and cut the best possible figure at the polls. Why should not the Labour or the Liberal party do that? He confessed he failed to see any difficulty if they had the system of voting so simple that he who ran might read and understand it. If the Labour man could vote" 1" for the Labour party and "2 " for the Liberal party and the Liberal " 1 "for the Liberal party and " 2" for the Labour party, they would get a consensus of progressive opinion and would be relieved from the absurdity which they saw at Crewe, where a minority—and he ventured to say the least thoughtful minority in the constituency—claimed the seat. (Applause.) "We shall have to get rid of that difficulty by the next election, added Mr. Crosfleld. (A VOICE : The sooner toe better.") Yes, I agree, the sooner the better, because when we have done that we can each in our own line do our best—and do it without any ill-feeling between us." (Applause.) Continuing, Mr. Crosflelci I laid emphasis upon the width and comprehensiveness of the Liberal party and pointed out how the various sections were doing real good work. There were the groups representative of advanced and moderate opinion in the Literal party, while there was the special obliga- tion upon the Labour party to study the interests of labour. What they had to ensure was that the whole of those progressive forces were united by the alterna- tive vote, so that they could give an even better account of themselves at the next election. (Loud applause.) He noticed that on that very mernorible clay in political history—lnsurance Day—they had a splendid meeting at NVarrington. (Hear, hear.) was thankful to think that in Lancashire, both employers and workers

KNEW WHEN THEY HAD GOT A GOOD THING (Hear, hear). They always anticipated that therd would be a little difficulty in the country for the first few months, before the benefits began to tell, but that difficulty would disappear quickly enough and we should only wonder how it was possible for millions of people in a great industrial country like ours to have got along without such a scheme, when we bad enjoyed its advantages for a time. (Applause). Calling attention to a few of the fictions which the Tories were circulating, Mr Crosfield said it had been asserted that the friendly , societies would lose their reserve funds. The truth was that the Act doubled those funds, throwing some .00,000,000 free for the increased benefit, of their members. (Applause). There was another piece of false coin he would like to nail to the counter. The Tories had stated that an insured person would get only half the benefits that would be given for the same money by a well-managed friendly society. The truth was that in order to get the same benefits as the Act gave, a friendly society would have to charge, accord- ing to age' a weekly contribution of from 7d. to Is. 3d. instead of the 4d. a week charged under the Act. (Applause). The third allegation they made was that an insured person who was already a member of a friendly society had to pay 4d. a week under the Act, in addition to what he now paid his friendly society. The truth was that he had to do nothing of the kind. (Applause.) It was also said that the insured person's 4d. a week went to pay the salaries of members of Parliament—(laughter)—ho (Mr. Crostield)was not. drawing anything just now—laughter) —and of the officials who worked the Act. As a matter of fact, every penny of the insured persons' • contribu- tions went to their insurance and to that alone. (Applause.) Having read what was said by Front Bench men on the Conservative side when the Insurance Bill came before Parliament, and remembering their declara- tion that here was a great national measure of social reform in which mere party work ought not to be allowed to interfere with genuine patriotism, he con- fessed to being amazed at THE DEPTHS TO WHICH TORYISM IN THESE DAYS HAD SUNK. . _

(Hear, hear.) There wad a declension of Toryism just now that was really remarkable. (A VOICE: "What can you make of it. " ? He did not know what to make of it. or where on earth the Tories stood. First of all they growled becaused the Government introduced pensions on a non-contributory basis and now, because they could not tackle the question of National Insurance without some division of contribu- tions between the State,the employer and the employed, they grumbled at that. When the Government brought forward the Insurance Bill, the Opposition said" glite right. We will back it up." Now Lord Robert Cecil said : " Oh, no. We will make this Bill different when we come in and we will have a non-contiibutory and voluntary scheme." It was one contradiction after another, not only on the Insuranne Act but on every- thing else. (Hear, hear.) In an allusion to

ROME RULE, Mr. Crossfleld said that in the debates on that measure the Tories had actually voted against the supremacy of the Crown in Ireland and against having any Secand Chamber at all in that country. He must say that on the point of consistency in reference to Tory principles, that fairly took the bun or, as Arthur Roberts used to say, romped in with the buttered crumpet. (Laughter.) It was extraordinary that in what they thought to be tactics the once great Tory party could descend to that kind of work—declension, contradiction and inconsist- ency all rolled into one. Reverting to the Insurance question, Mr. Crosfleld said one feature of the Act deserved special emphasis and that was the direct influ- ence it would have on the whole question of health and housing. For many years past we had heard a great deal of talk about social retorm, and he was right glad of it. It had been said that humanity of a sensible and reasonable kind was the best part of the thousand and one religions under the sun, and for his part he thought that those who held that iew were not very wide of the mark. He felt that the social reform which was before us and other democratic States at the present time ought to appeal not only to the democrat, the social student or the politician but to the

div.head: GREAT: RELIGIOUS BODIES
div.p: GREAT: RELIGIOUS BODIES

of the various countries. What was the of preach- ing sp:ritual advancement and progress, unless they had some reasonable amount of bodily comfort and well-being to build upon ? (Applause). It was being increasingly realized as years sent on what a disgrace to England our slum population was and how excessive were the extremes between wealth and poverty. In the Insurance Act they had a direct effort to deal with those problems at once. He believed our statute book was loaded with measures on the subject of the health of the community but they were not put into force— they had remained to a large extent a dead letter. If they looked at the way in which the Insurance Act was worked out, they would see how it was capable of remedying the evils of bad housing and insanitary con- ditions in populous centres. If an Insurrance Committee found that sickness in a district exceeded by 10 per cent, what might be calculated as a fair average, they had power to bring home the responsibility to the pro- per party—whether it be an individual employer of labour, a company employing labour, a landlord or a civic authority. Compensation could be demanded and if the person or authority concerned refused to pay it, the Local Government Board and Homo Secretary could be approached to bring pressure to hear. Only two days , ago an experienced permanent official in London—and I they were not always the most Liberal type, by a good I deal—told him : " The more I look into this insurance Act, the more I am impressed with the colossal blunder the Conservatives in England are making in thinking that Mr Lloyd George is only an imaginative orator and in failing to recognize the immense statesmanship he ponesses." (Applause). It was rather striking to get testimony of that kind from .an impartial, cool, calculating official whose business it was to study in cold blood the statistics and the practical working of Acts of that kind. When they saw a man fighting as hard as Mr. Lloyd George was fighting for the good of the mass of the population, it behoved them to give him an enthusiastic backing. I (Applause.) Only a few months ago his wife and he had the privilege of entertaining the Attorney General (Sir Rufus Isaacs) and Mr Lloyd George—(applause)— just after they had finished about twelve months' work on the Insurance Act, and he heard, from the Attorney General a great deal of the vat.y in which they had to devote their time and energies to that measure. It was not merely a question of length of hours—of having to work" from early morn to dewy eve "—for they were dealing with two men who notoriously were the most expeditious, rapid aid capable workers we ever had i

the House of Commons. (Applause.) They had just put in about twelve months at toe highest pressure on that Bill, and he would not in a hurry forget the tribute paid by that great barrister, now the Attorney. General, to the genius, initiative and energy of his colleague, Mr. Lloyd George. (Applause.) Tnere was another important election pending in North-West Manchester. What he wished to emphasise as that none of the workers in the Progressive Labour League should make the mistake of thinking they could take it easily as regarded the

GREAT FUNDAMENTAL CONTROVERSY which, after all, was still the chief issue between the forces of reaction and the forces of progress in this country. They must not think they had done with the question of Protection. It was perfectly true that in the first round or two Free Trade had given Protection a pretty good dusting, but they had not yet got borne with toe "knock out." Speaking as an advanced Liberal, he said in all sincerity that if the great pro- gressive army that backed up the best democratic Government we bad ever bad in power, had only got the great and sacred cause of Free Trade to unite them, be earnestly submitted thit that one bond of union was sufficient to excite their sustained enthusiasm— (applause)—and to deserve their incessant vigil- ance and staunch, spirited support. The Confederites had been telling members of the Tory party "If you don't stand for Protection, you must go out. We won't have you." Another section of the Tory party in London—and the wiser section too—were shaking their heads over the question of food taxation. They felt, as Lord Hugh Cecil had expressed it in his book, that the imposition of that kind of taxation on the population in these days was indeed a little I,hort of

HEADING FOR REVOLUTION and they did not fancy it. It was quite possible that the Goitederites would have their way, but there was also he possibility that a compromise might be effected in the Tory party, and that they might come forward at the next general election and say : "We are rp,t ssking you to vote for feed taxes, but only to supper t the appointment of la Royal Commis- sion, if we are returned." (A Voice: " Tory tactics ) Yes, there would be tactics to get their votes for food taxes under cover of a Royal Com- mission. Anybody who followed the figures of our trade sill who perused the comments on Protection in the foreign press. would begin to won- der bow that precious propaganda was ever sprung upon

its in 11103. He (the speaker)'was speaking to a Tory in London only the previous day and ventured to express amazement that the Tory Party could ever have become responsible for such a piece of foll3.The reply was" Joe had got to cover up the South African war' —(laughter) and,to tell them the truth, that was rather letting the cat out of the bag. (Laughter.) They in Warrington had to be on their guard against soch manceuvres as he had indicated. Defence of Free Trade was DO excuse for not pressing forward those other great causes which in a genuine way would gradually and steadily help to raise the level of civilzation for our people. It was their bounden duty, their highest duty and their greatest honour as progressives to work for social reform but they were not going to be so foolish, while they were engaged in that effort, as to let the Tories induce them to take that drtadlul step backward into Protection which would poison the whole of our public life and attack the well-being of the women and children. (Loud applause). Mr CARADOC REES began his speech by recalling his visits to Warrington with the Sefton cricket club twenty years ago when the late Mr Sydney Crosfleld captained the Warrington eleven. Applying cricket parlance to the nolitical situation, Mr Rees said that in the Crewe Divisions tbe Liberals had not been bowled—they had been run out. (Laughter) The Labour party called the Liberal party for a short run or vice versa ; they cut it a bit too Hue and they lost the wieket. They knew very well that if either the Liberal or the Labour party had been willing merely to keep its end up and allow the other one to make the runs, either of them would have won. He was not going to blame either of those parties. Everyone had a right to push his own cause at an election and what was wanted was some system of alternative vote or second ballot, so that the man who was returned to Parliament should in reality represent the division to which he belonged. (Applause). The Conservative party were welcome to any warmth they could get from the Oldham and Crewe results. Mr Bonar Law said the victory at Crewe was the

div.head: RISING SUN OF CONSERVATISM._
div.p: RISING SUN OF CONSERVATISM._

(Laughter). In reality it was the mere flickering of the flame of the bonfire of Conservatism. (Laughter and applause). The differences within the progressive forces were not a sign of weakness but of strength. Unity was strength only when there was diversity in the units. The Tory minstrels were appearing at Blenheim on Saturday. (Laughter). There they were on the platform—Cornerman Carson at one end and Tambourine Smith at the other. (Laughter). "What is the difference" asked the centre man of Bro. Carson " betweeu you and Smith?" "Give it tip" said Carson. "Well " was the reply" One has his tongue in his cheek and the other has his cheek in his tongue." (Laughter.) The Conservatives would never make very much as political tipsters, but they were continually trying it on. They said Home Rule would never be introduced in the House of Commons, hut it was introduced. (Applause.) They said Mr Churchill would never go to Belfast to speak. He went to Belfast and he spoke. (Applause.) The Hisestab- lishment Bill, they alleged, was merely a device for window-4ressing and would never be introduced. It had taken introduced. (Applause.) The Insurance Bill, we were told, would never come into force on July 15th on any account. But it did come into force, and very quietly too. (Applause.) Then they began to spread rumours that Mr Asquith and Mr Lloyd George or Mr Churchill were quarrelling for the leadership. (Laughter.) Such stories were only to be expected. The men who betrayed Mr Balfour expected the Liberals to assassinate Mr Asquith, but the men in ' the Liberal Cabinet were honourable men. (Applau.e.) As soon as this Government came into power in 1906 matters went forward. Up to that time we had had a Cabinet, as a rule, of Peers,but in 1:106 we got a Cabinet from the people of this country. (Applause.) The result was that measures for the benefit of the people were brought in and a feature which was unparalleled in the last 100 years was that in their appeals to the country the Liberals won three victories in succession. (Applause.) The Tories said the Government had no mandate for what they were doing. What did they think they were knocking the House of Lords down for ?—merely to do a bit of pointing here, to round it off there, and then to stand by and say, "Look what a beautiful job we have done'? They had taken that barrier out of the way in order to carry great measures through. (Applause.) Referring to the Insurance Act, Mr. Rees said the more they debated it the better. What was the fundamental principle of the measure? Not that they got ninepence ' for fourpence. He sincerely hoped they would give their four pences and never get anything—(laughter)— because he did not want any of them to be ill. (Applause). The underlying principle of the Act was each for all and all for each. (Applause.) Let them ask the other side what was their alternative to the Insurance Act (A voice : "Nothing.") The workhouse was all they had to offer. The man who grumbled about paying the super-tax should remember that if a man, his wife and four children went to the Workhouse, they cost the country £2 Els, a week. Under the Insurance At the man would be enabled to tide over periods of difficulty and to keep his children without having the mark of the Workhouse upon them. (Applause.) Dealing with the difficulties

which arose through the int roduction of labour-savieg machinery, Mr Rees said steps should be taken 1,4? ensure that those few who were displaced for the benefit, of the nation as a whole, should be helped until thex got some equally good employment. (ApP!aus)e• e the measures of Mr Lloyd George, he continued, we.rt permeated with that idea that more humanity come into our politics if they were to be of real Yalu% (Hear, hear.) It was in that spirit that he had brought'. old age pensions and national insurance. The Con servatives were fond of saying that Mr Lloyd Genrg° was a popularity hunter, always anxious to find small thing to tickle the palates of the multitude. Wn° w 0 Africa it who stood alone at the time of the South war, who faced hatred and political obloquy, wh7i seemed to wreck his whole political career ? It It the man who stood true in the hour of darkness they could trust in the day of victory. (Applause:) for had not trusted him in vain, because he was doing them now exactly what he woulel have like to have bee- done for him when he was a poor boy, lighting his wg alone. (Applause.) div.head: ECONOMICS. LABOOR-TIME A COMMODITY. PROFIT.
div.p: ECONOMICS. LABOOR-TIME A COMMODITY. PROFIT.
ARTICLE 11.

In a previous article we saw that a com- modity was something which was useful and which contained labour—that is, required labour for its production. We see that labour-time fulfils these two conditions. Labour-time is useful to the buyer of it and the labour spent in its production is the labour contained in the food, clothing and shelter consumed by the labourer. Now as labour-time is a commodity it follows that it must come under the law which determines the values of commodities in general. That law, given in the first article, is as follows:—" The value of a com- modity is determined by the necessary labour- time required to produce it." At first sight there appears to be some confusion here. How can the value of labour-time be determined by labour-time? What is the value of ten hours labour-time expressed in labour-time? Let us see. The value of a commodity (or its exchange rates with other commodities) is determined by the labour- time consumed in its production. Now what is the labour-time consumed in the production of ten hours of labour-time? Obviously it is the time used or consumed in producing the commodities which keep the labourer for ten hours. The value of living , labour-time is the value of the crystalised labour-time in the commodities consumed. If the average value of a day's labour is 3d. or 6d. that sum will exchange for commo- dities which will keep the labourer for a day. But the value created by the worker in that day may be much more than that consumed by him. This is the origin of profit. Let us now consider the process of com- modity production. Wealth is produced from nature by men working with machinery. A machine is a commodity, and on the average it exchanges on an equal basis with other commodities. As a machine wears out, its value passes to the commodity it helps to make. But there is no increase in this passing over—it is merely a change of form of value. If, say, a boot machine wears out while it helps to make 500,000 pairs of boots, it is obvious that one five-hundred-thousandth of its value has passed into each pair of boots. Labour is ultimately the source of all wealth, a machine simply stores labour. Well, our worker commences work and, using a machine, he adds value to the com- modities passing under his hands. While he is doing this, other workers, clerks, fore- men, managers and so on are also adding value to the same commodity. Note that the value added is quite distinct from the values created by previous workers and also from that added by the machine and other workers working concurrently. In the first Tart of the day the worker creates value equal to that which he con sumes in a whole day. In the second part he creates the surplus value which is the source of all interest, rent and profit. If the worker (all kinds of worker is included in this term) did not produce more than he consumed it is clear there could be no profits. it is not the function of economics to treat of the motives,interests or rights of any body of persons. It is simply concerned with an analysis of that which is. Economics should be an expert witness giving impartial evid- ence before all men and not a biased .sorvant dragged in to bolster up the theories of interested parties. Now economics declares that profit is the difference between the value produced by the worker and the value con- sumed by him. Let us see how different parties regard this question of profit. The capitalist says that profits are the wages of capital. In other words capital earns profits just as labour earns wages. But capital is no use unless it is in the form of machinery. Now the value in machinery is simply stored up labour-time and as the machine wears away the value passes into the commodity it is helping to produce. The value in the commodity is exchanged for a new machine and this goes, on indefinitely. If we consider the average ' firm we can see that the machinery in one sense is never worn away. I?eplacement for wear and tear does not come out of profits. Now if the machinery of a company is as good or better at the end of the year than it was at the beginning, how can it have produced profits? Again it is said that profit is the reward of abstinence. Because the owner does not uso it he is rewarded by an increase. Surely the reward of not consuming a thing to-day is that you will have it to consume at some future time and not that there will be more to consume. It is significant that this increase does not come unless somebody's labour is associated with abstinence.

Finally it is said that profits are the wages of ability. This is evidently untrue. Profit is that portion of wealth which is not con- sumed by the producers. Profit in any industry is only reckoned after all wages are paid. When a man turns his business into a company he receives two incomes, one salary as manager and the other profits as a shareholder. The brain worker then receives wages for his services while profits are received by owners simply in virtue of their ownership. It remains for us now to consider the other side. The Socialist readily agrees that labour creates all wealth, and that profits consist of that part appropriated by non- producers. Obviously this favours his argu- ment, so that he has no difficulty in accept- ing it, as had the capitalist. The Socialist says ;—" Labour produces all wealth; there- fore to the labourer it should belong." He calls the capitalist system robbery, and proves to his own satisfaction that it is very immoral. As a matter of fact it does not follow that the worker should have all the products of industry. The capitalist by paying the standard wage supplies the worker with means to restore the energy which has been spent by him. The worker has a commodity to sell, and the capitalist gives him the market value. Where is the robbery? Both capitalists and Socialists try to bring morals into a field which is essentially non- moral. We have had the old cry, "A fair day's work for a fair day's pay." Now what in practice is a fair day's work. Is it not as little as the employee can give while still retaining his job? And is not a fair day's pay as little as the employer can give while still keeping his men from leaving him? And now the Socialist and Syndicalist come along and demand everything. Somebody will have to think again. The walls of Jericho may have fallen down before a trumpet's blast but that doesn't seem to work with capitalism. Socialists and Syndicalists will have to do more than preach. Capitalism will disappear only when a more efficient system pushes it into oblivion, The only sure way of destroying is by creating some- thing better. A higher social system can only come through development of individual character, and preaching is impotent for this. Means will have, to be established for pro- viding the necessary human material, or morality and industry will come into no closer contact than they are at present. W. BA GULEY.

DISHONEST POSTMEN.

Of course I have nothing to say about the charge I itself, but the police court report of the case in which a young 1 cal letter carrier is involved brought to my mind quite a number of instances in which post- men in distacts in which I-have -been stationed have been convicted of tampering with packets entrusted to them for delivery, acd I have always marvelled at the simplicity of those who suprosed that such 135 stematic dishonesty could .for any length of. time continue undetected. They are so- common, however, that a separate department has to be maintained for the purpose of dealing with them, and exposure and di.grace inevitably ensue sooner or later. There have teen remarkable exceptiors, an old servant b,ing cccasionally convicted, but as a , rule the cffer.ders are foolishly young fellows who sorely lack experieree and commonsense. Of such as have come my way, I still have under observation two whose fall dates back several years, and to all appearance it has ruined them for life. The actual punishment of the crime on conviction is slight com- pared with the appalling after effects, the Cnce promising career being usually utterly spoilt. TEMPERANCE CAMPAIGN;

The speeches at the resumed temperance effort in the open-air were of the sort that act as a red rag to a bull to champions of "the trade." Speaking at the Midland Hotel, Manchester, at a licensed victuallers' banquet some time ego, the bead of a famous firm of whisky distillers warned the members that the last ditch had been reached. If, said he, the agitators who did not know the difference between a brev cry and an ice factory succeeded, blank ruin stared them in the face. "The thing aimed at is the extermination of your industry. Further compromise is impo;sible." There was nothing extraordinary abut the address thus far, but— and.this isby bow revert to the occasion—the orator went on to contrast with their temperance legis- lation what he presumed to be the inconsistmcy of the Goverament so far as

THE OPIUM4FRAFFIC was concet ned lie Mid be would like to refer these " would be social reformers" to a field which would show more fruitful results. Be had visited opium dens in China, the Orient, and ia the Pacific Islands, and he could say with all assurance that they were perfect bells. When the debate on the opium question came up in the House of Commons an honourable member said that they were playing the devil's game, and for every soul their missionaries sent to heaven the Government were sending ten to hell by this traffic. And for this he especially blamed the present Government because they seemed to cl tim right to all the moral and religious sentiments which existed. They forced China to take opium at 8 per cent import duty and charged 90 per cent. on the tea they sent them. " Consistency," added the speaker, " thou art a mule." The soap trust was dead— killed by public opinion. The opium trust thrived under all the machinery of a great Government. Let those who held up their hands in an indignant out- burst of morel rectitude against the licensed trade tare their attention to this perpetual exhibition of arbitrary Power encouraging and fostering this 'sordid business, violating ad the principles of humanity, and denying the victims the integrity of civilisation. The evil could be stopped at the very source where it generated, and this should he done at the India Office in Whitehall. Thus the great whisky producer. It is distinctly good in the light of more recent events—too good to be forgotten. UNWISE EXTREMES. Hot partisans, on both sides of this interminable drink controversy,are ever in danger of fanaticism and the display of bigotry and intolerance. The earnest fighters are sometimes carried by their feelings to ridiculous exttemes, and do harm to the cause they have Mayor of a certain borough gave a treat to the work- house inmatesand, ous' y espoused. Last Christmas the so amongst others who assisted in the musical part of the proceedings Was a Wesleyan choir. One of its selections was "Good King Wenceslas," but the monarch's hospitality proved too much for these pious souls. When it came to the line "Bring me flesh and bring me wine," the choir sang with extreme unction, "Bring me cake and ginger wine," thereby limiting the king's repast to the poor old peasant to their own narrow notions of good cheer.

"But, 'Sandy, mon„" objected the host " ye're not goin' yet, with the evenin' just started ?" "Nay," said the prudent MacTavish, "I'm no' goin' yet. DISTRESSING CASE AT WARRINGTON. A sad story was unfolded before Mr.' S.Brighouseand a jury at the Warringtou Coroner's Overt on Tuesday Mimi an inquiry was conducted into the circumstances surrounding the dea'h of Jeheph Wain Sims, u w.:rks foreman of 7, King Edward-street, whme body was found in a very decompcsed state in the river Money on Saturday. Harriet Selina Sims, the widowsaid they bad been married 18 years and up to six mouths ags had lived very happily together. During the past six in.mths sho had had reason to complain about her husband keep- ing late hours espscially on We'll' sday and Saturday nights. A few wet ks ago she received information that he was on familiar terms with is young woman, and in consequence a coolness sprang up ba,Aeen herself and her husband, who was a hasty and sharp-tempered man. Litterly he had not taken her into his confidence. About four o'clock on Saturday, June 22nd, he left home saying that he was going for a game of bawls. lie did not return until about 8 o'clock on the morn- ing of Monday, June 21th. Asked where he had been he said "if 1 told you, yoa would not believe me." Later he went out to work, and she did not see him alive again. Sce had since learned that he had stayed for the week-end in Manchtster in com- pany with the young woman, who knew he was a married man. On Saturday last Detec- tive-Sergeant Holland showed her a watch which her husband wds wearing whea he di appeared. . Alfred liamps.on, a wiredrawer at the kilter Matt res. Co., anl residing at 6, Greoubank-s•reet, said he had known the deceased or ab..mt 18 years. A few weeks ago he rensembered Mr. S:ms rind his wife laving words becanse she suspected him of being <it familiar terms with .another woman, lie had heard Sims con - plain about pains in the head, and he was a hasty tempered man. He had never heard him say be would take his I.fe. He had identified clothing and articles found en the body vs belonging to Sims. " Hector Sims (15), sou of the deceased, gave evidenle to the effect that at 2.30 pan. on the 21t1i June his father came in the house and told him to tell his -(witness's) mother that he was going to see a man at the works about tot turning in. lie added that he would not be long. He kissed the three children, and then went out in the direction of Manchtster-road. He had not sees his father since.

A pair of gloves was in the umbrella. lie also noticed footprints of a man's shoes extending to the river bank. The articles were afterwa•ds idmt I'd as the property of the deceased. In answer to the coroner witness said Ct.° umbrella would be 2ft. away from the water. • Joseph Shaw, lock keeper at Manor Lock, and living in a cottage near by said that at 11.80 on the 27th July he noticed a dirk object floating in the centre of the river and on getting a boat hook he found it was the body of a man since identified as that of Sinao. It was veryu e tneicutcihv edesceormg epaonsted. Holland said the features and shuil of the body were badly disfigured, possibly by passing flats. The Coroner in addressing tho jury said the moth c r of the girl with whom the deceased had been away in Manchester discovered the relationship existing between the ,couple and on the 2ith Jnne, after her daughter had been away with the man, she interviewed Sims at the works. He arranged that some explanntion should be given later in the day. lie never kept that appointment hut went home find kissed the children good-bye and went away. The jury would understand what his state of mind would be when in that fix. Mr. Lloyd George; accompanied by Mr. John Burrs and Mr. Masterman, receive,' a deputation at the House of Commons on Tuesday from the County Councils Association regarding the sanatoria provisions of the National Insurance Act. The Chancellor of the Exchequer said the Bill as introduced dealt with insured persons only, but was extended to insured persons and their dependents. fhe finance provided W3S £1,600,000 for capital charges and .C 1,000,000 a year for mainten- ance. That was not enough, andj the Treasury and county Councils must find the deficiency. Regarding consumptives who were neither insured nor dependents and were outside the Act he and Mr. Burns felt that the deputation were entitled to ask to what extent the , Government would meet a County Council in treating I the whole problem of consumption within its area.

HOW TIIEY DO THINGS IN JAPAN.

As we have all been reading something about Japan and the Mikado in the news- papers it may be appropriate to remind my readers of how the East differs from the West even in the smallest things. Japan is what we:should call a thoroughly left-handed country. Take just a few things. We shake hands with each other; in the East a man skakes hands with himself. We take off the hat on entering the house; they take off their shoes. If a woman wears a train to her dress she wears it at the front. Japanese books begin at the end, the word ' Finis ' coming where we put the title page. The foot-notes are printed at the top of the page, and the reader puts in his marker at the bottom. A Japanese mounts his horse at the right side. Boats are hauled up on the beach stern first. The Japanese do not say north-east or south-west, but east-north or west-south. • They address a letter in the reverse way to us, putting the name last, and instead of writing Mr. John Smith they put. Smith, John Mr. In keeping accounts they write the figures first, the items corres- ponding to them next._ _ _
Yes, Japan is a left-handed country. But when the Japs come here they think that we are the left-handed contrary folks, and who is to say which is right.

div.head: POEM WORTH LEARNING.
div.p: A POEM WORTH LEARNING.
Here is a serious little poem which is well worth learning:—

NOW. If you have a thing to do, Do it now. Other days will dawn, 'tis true, But they may not dawn for you ; Take no chances, put it threugh, Do it now. If you have a word to say. Say it new. Let no demon of delay Held you from the cherished way, Speak your bravest word to-day, Say it row. If you have a friend to bless, B! es him now. What avails the tenderness, What the rapture you profess, What the loyalty, unless ? Bless him now. Oh, the nrtrvel and the need, Here and now! Make these words a living creed, Turning thought and will to deed, Earth will turn to heaven, indeed, Here and now. GRUMBLETON. Folks who live in Grumbletown, Show a scowl and wear a frown, Never deign to give a smile, Mumble, grumble, all the while. Winds are always hot or cold, Making Grumble people scold; Fretting, fuming, they complain If it shine or if it rain. All their tempers are awry, Cannot please 'em if you try; Nothing right, and all things wrong— That's the burden of their song. If you live there, don't you stay! Pack your goods and move away; Look around—on every hand Shines the happy Laughter Land! . —Willis Warren Kent, THIS WEEK'S STORY. JOHNNY AGAIN.
Johnny: "Father, how would you punctuate this sentence, The wind blew the five pound note from off the table into the fire' ?"
Father (after careful deliberation) : "I should put nothing except a full stop at the end."
Johnny: 'Wouldn't you? I think I should make a dash after that five pound note."

div.head: UNION BANK OF MANCHESTER
div.p: THE UNION BANK OF MANCHESTER
LIMITED.

The seventy-sixth annual general meeting of the shareholders of the Union Bank of Manchester Limited, was held at the head ofllae of the Beak, York-street, Manchester, on Wednesday, the 31st July. TGe chair was occupied by Mr U C Haworth (chair- man of the 13 mk), who was supparted by Sir Chai lea Behrens (deputy-chairman), Mr J It Oliver, Mr Michael Cabad, Colonel C 11 France frayhurg. D.L., Mr AlMa II Bright, Sir Joseph Ye: din, Bart., D.L, and Mr P Forresier (general managEr). In m lying t-,e adoption cf the report, the Chairman said the gross profit shown is £83,816, and this balance is after sating aside an amount to cover income tax. You will observe tha tign:e jest named is £3,150 more than this time last year. After adding the amount b 'ought forwerd from the last profit end loss account we l ave a g 03S balance of 01,836. In common with other trades we have suffered by the labour troublt s hindering us from showing an increased profit. I may add, th 3 !auk rate has been somewhat unfavourable to nkt r . _ _

The annunt placed to bank premises account, reserve and peision funds are the scene 69 before, and we have again declared a dividedd of 12i per cent less income tax. After providing for all these items there is a balance to carry forward of £10,362, an increase of £2,300 compared with the previous half. Turning to the balance sheet, the most important change since we last met together is in the reserve fund. In our balance sheet for the Christmas half of 1911 we took from our reserve £50,000 for providing against bank's investments. The shrinkage of the market value of investments serves as a subject for dis- cussion at every half-yearly bank meeting throughout the Kingdom. As this has been continuous we felt sure that you would agree as to the advisability of maintaining our investments at the market price. All our investments rank as Trustee or gilt-edged securities and these, unfortunately, have suffered the most in depreciation. Current, deposit and other accounts stands at .C 3,150,239 and this shows a large increase as compared with the same time last year. It is a little less thin the total at the end of December, but, as I have frequently explained at those mcetings, our customers invariably require more money at the end of June than they d.) at the end of December, and there- fore the comparison, to be correct, should be made with the corresponding half-year. The progress in this item is gratifying to us, not only because it supplies the sinews of war "—namely, cash to lend in the usual charaleis of trade—but indic.ites clearly the continued and inmasing confidence of the public. We believe that iu the near future the amount of current and other accounts will be increased to six millions.

You will have observed that we are building new premises at Winsford ; the old building there is another evidence of what might be termed the business outgrowing the fabric. You will also notice we are opening a branch at Rawtenstall in the Rossendale Valley. The industrial unrest In our midst during the past twelve months is a matter that cannot be regarded with indiffer- ence, 'whether it be the railway strike of last autumn, the local and national dockers' strikPs, the coal strike of this spring, or the struggle existing at present at tLe London Docks. These are all causes of alarm, more especially as we have not found a remedy for such onslaughts upon our trade ' and commerce, our comfort and well-being. The National Insurance of the workpeople, the increased cost of materials of production, together with the advances in wages—all of thase, being equal to a tariff, will, I fear, handicap our industries. Hitherto, owing to the facilities for producing cheaply, we have success- fully competed with other countries in the neutral markets of the world, and held such markets as our own. May it continue so, and may we foster that posi- tion, maintaining with care and jealousy any encroach- ment on our proud posiHon. This, I venture to think, is our wish ; it is our wish, end is the real interest of the community at large. Referring to the past, and looking at the other and brighter aide of the picture, there are causes for congratulation. Our Imports and Exports both show increases ascoropared with former years. We are told that during the past six years we have reduced our National Debt by 61 millions, whilst , the reduction in France has been 17 millions, and Italy 10 millions. On the other hand Mr. Asquith tells us that Germany and Austria have increased their debts by 83 and 112 millions respectively. Mr. Barbour seconded and the resolution w s carried unanimously. Mr. George C Howarth and Mr. John R. Oliver were re-elected directors of the company.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
Resignation of Padgate Officials.

The fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Gusrdians was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday, Mr E L Bent presiding. There were also present . Mrs Simpson, Bess 'l' It Matthews and A M Mitchell, Messrs A J Jolley (deput..-chairman), W Gill, W Houghton, W C Brooss; W F ness, A Brooks, G Mather, It Lee, J A Rushworth, J A Hughes, W Flanagan, A Bottomley (clerk), It I Partridge (assistant clerk), 6 tad W J Brown (master). rAtritovamENr AT TB E WORKHOUSE. At a meeting of the Building Caramittee, the tender of Messrs atrford and Perkins, of Peterborough, for the supply and fixing of a cooking apparatus at a cost of £369 e.as accepted. The clzumitte also accepted the tender of Mr ti Bibby, of Wirriugton, t supply and fix electric light equipment at the Workhouse for the bum of £B9 15s.

S. PER BOTH. At a meeting of the House Committee the Clerk read a letter from the Superintendent of the County Police, Leigh, enclosing a letter issued to police authorities by the Home Wins in which attention was called to the serious annoyance and possible danger to the public by the onveyauce of verminous and dirty prisoners in public conve3ances, and suggesting application being made to the Guardians to allow such . prisoners to be cleansed at their institutions upon payment of an agreed fee. The Clerk reported that the Chief Constable of Warrington bad made a similar request. It was decided that tbe Borough and County police authorities be granted the use of the apparatus at the Workhouse for the cleansing of any verminous priners at a uniform fee of five shillings for every prisoner cleansed. The minutes were approved.

, RESIGNATION OF PADGATE OFFICIALS. • The CLERK read a letter from Mr. J:im Fairhurst, porter and induttrial trainer at the Padget° Cottage [Tomes, resigning his position after 30 years service. lie said he felt keebly his severancefrom the imtitation but he felt the time had arrivod when be must cease active cork, as anyone, on reaching his age, must find it impossible to give the duties the care and Attention they required. lie would be grateful if the Guardians could rise their way to Add a lea' years to his period of service in computing his superannuation a!lowance. Mrs. FartmultsT a rote resigning the oflice of portress and ruM.ing a &miler nog test. She pointed out that owing to the illness of the late respected matron she had been pelf !ruing extra duties for a con- s'deratle time. She was at present in receipt of the same salary as when she was appointed thirty yews ag?:

Mr MATHER prepz,sed that the resignation be accepted veith Er, at regret. TLe Board use losing a pair of officers %ho had been second to none in the kingdom—unerssuming, honest, trnthful, industrious, sober and always to be relied upon. Mr HOUGHTON seconded. He said Mr end Mr Fairhurst were too of the oldest officisls of the Union and ca ried out their duties r,e ith the strictest integrity and honesty. They had never been unwilling to do extra work, outside their obligations as officials. He hoped the Board would take a generous view of the case when tire time came to flx the superannuation. The Rev A M MITCHELL : This regret is rather , belated. You have had these cffilials thirty years and ' during the whole of that time you have not offered them a £5 note extra for their services. Then you come here and talk about them being excellent officers , and all the rest of it. Why in the name of common- sense didn't you give them more salary ? Mr. MATHER : Did you ever hear such nonsense from anybody ? Mrs SIMPSON : Well, lot it pass. Mr BU:11WoliTH : The position, I think, is amply, paid now. The resignations were accepted with regret. Mr W C BROOKS moved that the question of Boum-- annuat ion allowance and the appointment of a successor be referred to the Pildgate Cottage Homes Conamittea. Mr FLANAGAN gecOnded. 1 In the course of the discussion, the Rev A M MITCHELL interposed : You never gave her an extrrs Fenny for her labour. It is a shame. Mr JOLLEY : It is open to us to rectify that now. The Rev A M 111ITCHELL : Be liberal then. Ultima'ely the propothion was agreed to, on the understanding that the rec3ninwndation of the Cottage Homes Committee on the question of superannuation should afterwards be referred to the Finance Com- mittee.

TIIE INsURANCE ACT. The CLERK reported that he had approached the Insurance Commissioners to see if it wt r, possible to obtain exemptions from inturi nce for Om wives of certain officers of the Beard who held joint appoint- ments. lie had received a reply stating : If the joint silary of the married couplcs referred to is in respect or.work performed by both husband and wife, both will b 3 required to b. 3 insured, and for the • purposo of determining the rates of COE- trirution the salary should be apportioned according to the work performed by each. If any person Is ordinarily and mainly dependent orpon sine otter person for his or h( r livelihood, it will b 3 open to him, if he so desires, to claim a certificate of exemption I under section 2of the Act.. Such a certificate relieves the employee but not the employer, of the liability to pay coutritutions. The rneanin4 of the letter, said Lhe Clerk, was i hat all married officers would have to be insured. Even if exemptions had been obtainable the Board would have to pay their c,mtribution.

A I'OiIiICAL QUESTION. The CLERK reported the receipt of a letter from the Land Union calling the attention of municipal corpora- tions and railway authorities to the serious aspect, as regarded local rating, of the proposals of the single- tax party," who have apparently persuaded the Govern- ment to espouse their cause.' lie had read part of the letter when

Mr. A. BROOKS remarked : Are we not asked to CItS- CMS something which is beyond Poor Law and the Assessment Commit'ee and which is essentially a political matter ? It we begin to discuss this, or even bear the letter read, we must hear the other aide. I prop( se the letter be not entertained. Mr. Ilexottz N seconded. Every tub, he remarked, must stand on its own bottom. The CHAIRMAN: I read it and I thought it would be information for those who are members of the Assessment Committee. It is entirely in your hands. The CLERK said the Board did n generally consider anything verging on polical matters. It was decided not to proceed with the reading of the letter.

The peat part affected was my head. It became one mass of thick dry heaps of scurf.
