MISS SMITH'S LUGGAGE.
BY DORA LANGLOIS
Author of "The Crimson Slipper," "A Bolt from the Blue," "That Red-Headed Woman," "The Kiss of Judas," "Victoria's Dream," Au.

"It's tile most sensible thing I ever read," said Christ°bd. "Yes," I answered, dubiously, stealing glance at the paper to make sure that it was all there just as Christobel had read it out. Yes; there it was in cold print, an article by a famous lady doctor saying that one's summer holiday ought to be a complete chango, that one should dare to break away from the conventional, change one's name if one liLed, and go in search of excitement and adventure, to improve one's vital forces, and re-estsblish lest energy and vim. "It's 80 scientific and convincing," said Chris `.obel. "Y. s; but," I murmured, "isn't that about changing one's name rather—" "Of course it is," she answered. "That is the point of it. Suppose that we do chpnge our names, are we going to do anything wrong?" "I'm sure I hope not," I amented, hastily. "I only meant if we were found out—" "If we are doing nothing wrong it won't matter a jot! Dzsidco," she added, "any per- son of ordinary intelligence would .take good care not to be found out." . . .

"It's—it's meant as an experiment for people whese lives are dull," I suggested; and it secres to me that with us things are not 80 vcry—" "Oh of course," she retorted, "it's not meant for poor, contemptible, little-minded creatures whose aspirations ore bounded by petty rustic triumphs. ' What could I soy? I was really quite con- tented with life long before I happened to win the ladies' singles, and the first prize for fancy dress; but it's not easy to explain thaw' things, so when Christobel reminded me that it was her turn to arrange the form our holi- day should take I left it to her. "Where do you think cf going?" I asked. "I've not decided yet," she answered. "Beeitles, it would spoil the spirit of the thing to &souse details.' I agreed that that was so, but I thought it was carrying it rather too far when she went to bed on the ere of our departure without t2lling me our destination, or what train she meant to catch. Fortunately, all our trains have* go to the junction, so I was up in time to catch the first one. _ .
• " Dear !" 6he exe!ainied, es she hurried in to breakfast. "Are you starting by the 7.30? " _ . _
•.--. "I thought you might wish to," I ex- plained. "But good grscious ! you don't suppose _comii.g with we!" elle ejaculated.

"Why, of COLIT6;.-" I began. - "Are you going to pour the tea out, or shall I?'' she interrupted. "Didn't I ex- plain that the key-note of our holiday WM to be freedom from convention? How can it be if we go together? I risked you for a cup of tea, you needn't fill the saucer. Now when you've cp-ite finished mopping the table-cloth you can decide on a place to go to, and then you may come C. 6 far CES the junction with me if you are sure you have got everything ready,. for I've no time to help you." "I couldn't' make up my mind in the time," I cold, feebly, "I couldn't, really. I shall have to give it up, and go to Ramsgate later with Majorie and the children." I do not know why, but she got quite cross with me at once. She seemed to make it quite clear that my even thinking of going for my holiday with my cousin and `her brood" was enough to prevent women ever getting a vote. She said it was "treason to the cause," and particularly mean to her to back out of it after she had arranged to play a courageous part and defy the conventions. So when she finished by pointing out that women ought to hold, together, and that that was why we via st go on our holidays alone. I agreed to start by the 7.30 if she thought she could look up a place for me to go to, and think of a new name for me before UV got to the junction. She was' quite kind about it when -she saw my difficulty, and said it would not give her any trouble; in fact, when I npolog:sed che explained that she would not think of "mak- ing a trouble" of a little thing like that, and long before we got to the junction she had de- cided that I should go to Aberystwyth (it's quite near the top of the ABC index), nnd had invented a new name for me aim The name w;-s Smith. _ _ .

Christobel has a wonderful head for detail. "I saw that your boxes weren't labelled," rue romance.d, ."ery as I've got some luggage- tags I'll write them for you. 'Mks Hilda Smith, passenger to Aberystwyth.' We will tie them on at the junction, and that will ratify the compact; for, of course, as I am not going to use my own name, you mu6t pro- mi6e most solemnly not to use yours."

I gave the promise. " It will be strange at first," she admitted, "to get used to being called Mies Smith, bul sC/011 get accustomed to it. You must remember that we are doing a great deal to benefit womankind, .and all you have to do is

to keep it a secret." She added that she could have said a great deal more to make me feel easy in my mind if she had not been so worried about her hat- box; but she found time to tie the labels on for me before the London express came in and carried her away. I had an hour to wait for the train going Wcst, and altogether it was a dreadful Jour no. None of the trains fitted, and when got there at last it was not Aberystwyth rs all. but Barmouth.

Ihe porter was a Welshman. He said there was a train to Aberystwyth in half on hour, and that as it was a mistake they would not charge me anything. I thought Barmouth looked rather nice, GO I said it did not matter much, and that I thought I would stay where I was, and pay the difference, if he could get my luggage for- warded. "What tame, miss?" he asked. And before I had time to think I bad an- swered: " Miss Hilda Meadows."

"And Wa6 your name on the boxes?" he inquired. "They—they are addressed to Mice Smith," I (stammered. "And Miss Smith, has she come with you indeed?" "No-o, I— She didn't; I came here 21one " I answered. "Then Mies Smith will be at Aberystwyth with the boxes in the meanwhile?" he re- marked. "Oh, no!" I exclaimed. you see—she did not conic." "But the boxes will he Mice Smith's boxes," be persisted. "They are not here, they are mine." I cried. "That is. they sometimes-- You see. we both use them."
"The fact is—

"But if they are for Miffi Smith at Aberystwyth," be objected, "we hove no in- structions and direction to fetch them here." "It doenn't matter," I answered, with studied dignity. "If you can't oblige me, I will go on to AberyBtwyth and get them my- self."

I was naturally annoyed nt the man's ob- stinacy, and I thought it very rude when, half an hour later, he brought the stationmaster Up to the carriage I had entered, and both of them stared at me, nnd walked off whispering. However, when I got to Aberystvyth I vent to the inquiry-office quite boldly, con- sidering that I knew I must be looking shoo. ing, and asked for luggage addressed to Miss Hilda Smith. There was quite an important official there. "I am sorry to tell you that me have had several luggage thefts on this line lately," he remarked. "I am informed that you are known at Barmonth by the name of Meadows. Ts that true, and if so, can you ex- plain it?" "Certainly," I answered. "You set, the fact is—" And I was just going to tell him everything, when I remembered my rolemn prom jar. " W ell? " he said, in a peremptory kind of voice. There was tabsolutely no time to think. It was 0114 of 'those dreadful emerocticico.. You

"r have friends here," "1 replied, pointedly. "May I?" he asked, and sat down beside me. "Lovely place this! Have you decided where you are going to stay?" "1 em .going to stay here on this beneh," I responded, hotly, till I've got over; the shock of the invidious pcsition you've 'eon= trived to place me in." I certainly expected him to try to defend %is conduct, and argue that it was not his fault, and ea that sort of thing; but he did not. _

"I seem to have made a mess of it some- how," he admitted. "By the way, I know quite the best btarding-house in the town, and it's on my road. Will you come and have a look at it?' In justice to him I must state that he was very discreet. He looked the other way and hummed a tune till I stopped crying, and then we started for the bearding-house. "I'll arrange it all, and tell them you've lest your luggage," he said. Os we reached the door. "By the way, is it Mies Meadows or Miss Smith?" "Miss Smith!" I answered, decidedly, for I was not going to let him think I had no will of my own. I cannot tell you what a wretched time I had the following, day. If having "excitement and adventures' means only one frock and no sunshade, no one of any sort speaking to you at the boarding-house, and people of all sorts speaking to you on the pier—then I do not care for it. And Mr. Dixon did not call, and I could not see him on the esplanade or anywhere. It was late in the afternoon when we met by accident, and again he shewed surprise at finding Inc alone. "I suppose you expected to see me accom- panied by the police? ' I remarked, scorn- fully. „

"'Not at all," he answered. "Far from it, I assure yon." "I thoupt you might be staying indoors not to witness the painful scene of my arrest," I said. "The fact is," he explained, "I did not call because-- Well, don't you see, Miss Meadows's frionds are my friends, but Miss Smith's friends might consider me de trop." "I have told you I've no friends here," I replied, angrily, and, what's more, I didn't. expect to meet anyone. You mustn't suppcse because I ..was a little up.set about my luggage that I had any other disappointment. It's a truly horrid idea, and I'm much obliged to you for entertaining it I" " I apologise," he said; "but, naturally, when you arrived alone under an assumed—l mean, under such remarkable eircumstancrs. I thought that you had come to meet some--- Well; any way, what happened at the station waa. enough to shew me that dis- cretion is the best policy, and that services offered with the best intentions are not al- ways acceptable." "You need not allude to the 'best policy'," retorted, stiffly. "It is quite unnecessary to remind me that Honesty is tho best policy '. Of course, being n man, you will take the worst pccsible view of everything. You naturally think that if a woman doesn't go about labelled with the same name as her father or her husband, she is bound to lcse her dignity—" "Or her temper, or her luggage," inured. he mur-

I got up. "I am glad you find tho situation amusing,' I said. But, personally, I see nothing to laugh at in being under suspicion and baying only one frock to wear." "It seems a very pretty frock," he com- mented; "and surely one can always pur- chase a few nernssarics? One does not need much at the seaside." "If I tried to replace one-third of the really necessary things that I have lost I should leave myself without any funds at all," I an- swered, scornfully. "I am .very sorry," he stammered, "If I were not quite so much in the dark--" "Upon what subject, pray?" I demanded. "The reason of the incognito?" he ex- plained. "I shall certainly not court trouble by venturing to make another guets." "I bare already told you that them waa no reason," I replied. "The joke, then?" he said. " If 1 could see the point of it I might stand a chance of making the officials se it. "It wee not a joke," I interrupted, hotly. "It was an experiment, a solemn compact be- te•cen myself and a friend." ell'auld like to that, friend," he
at ainn2r, ana answerca in monosytiabtes, and looked bored when the other women changed their minds and fried to talk to me.

On- the whole, the next few days were not unpleasant. Mr. Dixon called regularly, and as I knew nothing of the town or district, took it upon himself to shew me all the nice places, which was really very unselfish on his part, as be had only a few days of his awn holiday left. With his help I really "did Aberystwyth" thoroughly. But there was one street that he was meet anxious we should avoid. It was not a slum either (there are no slums in the town), but quite a nice -looking, respectable street. I said I thought it looked all right, but he said that "looks were not every- thing," and that for all he knew there might be a case of scarlet fever in one of the houses, so I came to the conclusion that he was put- ting it that way not to alarm me too much, and agreed to give the place a wide berth. The last day of his short stay had arrived before either of us bad occasion to visit the railway station again. We only went then be- cause I was anxious to visit one or two of the more distant show-places, and be would insist on my going while he was able to accompany me. He was very much .flushed, and looked dreadfully nervous when he went to get our tickets, but / rather enjoyed it, for I saw the horrid official looking at me, and I knew that the perfect fit of my gown must prove even to a man that the boxes and their contents were my very own property. . _

- "Do you know, my companion said, when trt last we were seated, and the train had started, "I should feel very much more com- fortable if you would leave Aberystwyth, and spend the rest of your holiday with friends? "

" I really can't see why I should," I re- plied, with quiet dignity; " though, of course, I understand that you would like all women to how to the conventions. You think that wo,nen in general " " I don't think anything about women in general," he retorted, rudely, " and I don't care either I'm thinking about you. We have had marvellous luck so far, but posi- tively sometimes I have been afraid to turn the corner of the street for fear of catching sight of someone. _

"Oh ! yes, I know," he* continued, cutting me short in an acid retort. " Your motives an; very noble, and all the rest of it; but if you meet a person, and lie is on age other side of the road, and he merely bows and passes on, or, worse still, doesn't bow and looks the other way—you—you can't explain your motives at the top of your voice, can you? It's useless to say you don't mind being misunderstood, because you were disagreeable enough to me about it—and---and, take it en the whole, it's the most insane and idiotic proceeding I ever heard of, and it can't goon! " " Pray do not concern yourself any further with my affairs," I said, when Ile paused for breath. " I can't get out of the train while it is in motion, of course, but as soon as pos- sible I will relieve you of the risk of being seen with me."

" You are purposely aggravating," he re- plied; " but you have got to answer my ques- tion. Are you or are you not going back to your friends? " " Certainly not, at the dictation of a rerson who has no right to _interfere," I answered.

" Very well, then," he said stiffly, "if you insist on remaining in Aberystwyth, perhaps you had better khow how I got your boxes for you." " Pardon me," I interrupted, " I refuse to he lectured and dragooned; but, as it hap- pens, I made arrangements to leave to- morrow some time ago." " You are not leaving to go anywhere else as Miss Smith? " he queried, sharply. " I am leaving and going home, because I find the place dull," I explained. "I am sorry you have found it so dull," he remarked, in a tone of offence.
"It is a matter of no consequence," I re- plied; " but now that I have explained my motives to^ departure, perhaps you will be good enough to tell me how you obtained my 9 " •

"Really, I don't know that it is worth while !" he said, evasively. " It's no use going into all that now that you are going home." " I don't like mysteries," I remarked, " and I must insist, Mr. Dixon, on your tell- ing me all about it." " Oh ! it was very easy," he said. " Easy? " I queried. " Quite !" he answered. " I—l just told the railway men what I knew they would believe."

" And what was that, pray? " " Well, it was practically what you told them yourself—about changing your name when you left home." " They didn't appear to believe nie," I said. " No," he answerod. "It all depends on the explanation ; and, you see, you didn't ex- plain it." " And may I efdt hew you explained it?" I demanded. "I offered them the explanation that had occurred to me," he answered, looking steadily out of the window. I sat up with a gasp. " Then you said " I said that, of course, they would see how it was—and I tipped them a sovereign—that was all." _ . _

" You implied that I had come here alfme to mcet someone—in fact, to meet you? " • " Anyhow, they wouldn't have believed any other story," he muttered, obstinately. " It was abominable ! " I panted. "They ware just going to wire to Honey Hill, to make all sorts cf inquiries," he ob- served. " Mr. Dixon," I said, " you have compro- mised me most shamefully! You have violated every--every " " Convention? " he suggested. " No. Every—every rule of conduct," T corrected him. " You have behaved like a— like a " " I deny it," he said. " What do you mean?" I asked. " The fact is," lie explained, " I haven't pt a woman's courage ; I'm horridly afraid of the conventions-1 mean the rules of con- duct. It would make me most uncomfortable to fly in Mrs. Gruady's face, and I simply didn't attempt it." What did you do? " I asked, faintly. " I made the best story I could of it," he arimered. " I said we had known each other

..... fory.:•ars—and that it had been a very long engagement—and that your trustees were brutes—and that, in short, you had run away from line to get married to me as soon as the regist-:r would do it." "I ean never, never go back to Aberyst- wyth," I whispered. " There are other placc3," ha answered , " thoup,h I don't agree with you that the town is dull." _ _ _ _
' I shall go straight to London from the next station,'' I announced. " Your boxes can he emit after you," he acquimmed. "And I shall tell Cousin Marjorie all about Mr. Dixon ! "
" Naturally, Miss Meadows." "oh, Oil " I panted, recalling the inte- rested glances I had encountered at the station. "I wonder if the railway men be- _

lieved you? " "I did my best to make them," he said. grimly. " You see, unfortunately it turned out that the wretched official lived next door to the, refii,trar. his office 1.: as in that street, you know." " Well? " I queried, quite unable to follow him. " And the law demands that the registrar's notice-board should be placed in a prominent position." " And you—" I panted. " I had to!" he answered; and now ht stopped examining the scenery, a turned and looked at me. It was one of those dreadful momcots when a bodice made to fit an elephant would hays been all too small to hold me and all feelings. They crowded up into my throat., and found some vent in a wordless, fearful gasp. His voice sounded a long way off, and I never sat behind an engine that panted so loudly and made such a 'fearful vibration. "Please .',.observe that the announcemaut hinds you to nothing—to nothing at all, Miss Meadows." I collected myself with an effort. "Of course it doesn't, Mr. Dixon." " Unless—unless you like," he whispered.

I started for London from the very next station. I decided to travel alone, but I fancy that Walter—l mean Mr. Dixon—inter• viewed the guard, and put me in his charge. He followed me by the next train. Cousin Marjorie was awfully surprised when I burst in upon her unexpectedly, huf she was very sweet about it. She aliered her arrangements, And took me and the children to Ramsgate at once. Walter joined us there, and did not seem to mind the babies and the donkeys one bit.

Christobel had retu:ned from her holiday some time before I got back. I cannot say that she looked any better for her change of air; she seemed to have contracted sonic kind of slight nervous ailment, and appeared to be always in the condition one is in when one ex- pects a servant to drop a tray. She was not very sympathetic about my engagement, or the troubles I had gone through. She said that people were not fit to be "pioneers of re- form" who could not even manage their own little affairs.
I asked her how she had enjoyed her holi- day. She Raid she had enjoyed it i.-nmensely, but she would not tell me where sb a bad been or anything about her adventures. [Tisi END.j

know, that happen to Generals and Admirals and Prime Ministers; and no one ought to judge too harshly—for it must be conceded that I got as near the truth as possible. I said: "The fact is, my name is Smith, but when I am on my holidays I prefer to call myself Miss Meadows." I really think the man was convinced (per- haps he would not have been had I put it the other way), and I was just congratulating my. self when a voice behind me said: "What's the matter? Can I be of any service?" And, turning. I found myself face to face with Walter Dixon. He was one of the judges at our fancy-dress carnival, and I used to think him such a sen- sible man. I had no time to speak, however, no time to do anything but wonder what would happen next, when the horrid official addressed him. "The lady claims some luggage," he explained, "and we want prcof of her identity." That's a simple matter!" Mr. Dixon re- joined. "I've known the lady for years. She is Miss Meadows, of Ryecroft House, Honey Hill. Which is her luggage?" "You are quite sure, then, that her name is not Smith?" "Smith? Not a bit of it!" he answered. "Who ever said it was?" The official turned to me. "We can't let you have the articles addressed to Miss Smith: he said. "The case is clearly ,one for further inquiry." - "Very well," I answered; and bowing stiffly to, Mr. Dixon, I walked away. I virlked straight out of the station, and went on till I got to the esplanade. The guide-books will tell you all about the esplan- ade; visitors say it is particularly nice aftet dunk. I did not notic3 ita beauties. I had plenty to think about in my dreadful situa- tion, but I could not think of anything ex- cept the remarks I would make to Mr. Dixon about his unwarrantable interference with my affaira. I had been sitting there a qnarter of an hour, perhaps, before _the horrid idea dawned on me that he had deserted me, that erhape he was not coining after all! It was a few minutes after that that I caught sight of him. "What, all alone, Miss Meadows!" he ex- plainuvl iiscwiar't vnur friendo met your'
said. "Just a teff- minutes' interviTW. tioull be enough " ; and he bit a pebble with hie stick and sent it spinning into the sea. " She is a very fascinating woman," I remarked.

lie paused in the net of assaulting snot/ter pebble, and glanced at me out of the corner of his eye. "She would not have lost her luggage or her dignity," I continued. " Doubtlers she would have retained her entire stock of both commodities," be an- swered.

"She would not have lest her temper either," I asserted. "She would have treated the rudeness of ill-bred people with the con- -empt it merits. She does not allow herself to be upset by trifles." "I can quite believe that," he aasented. "Of course, you can't be expected to un- derstand it," I said, "but she had the best interests of her sex at heart—"
"In propceing that you ehould aispera• with such encumbrances ae a name and a chaperon?" he queried. "Exactly!" I retorted. "And what was the abject of the experi- ment?" he Asked. _

"Why, to ehew how easily one can do with- out them," I answered, proudly. "Oh, ah, yes; of course," he said. "You must excuse my stupidity. Now, about that lest lugirge of yours? If I were to explain to the officials—" _ _

"I don't see what right they have to know my motives," I objected. 'None whatever," he agreed. "I was only asking for my own information. One must thoroughly understand a situation before one attempts to explain it." But I can't possibly allow you to repeat what J have told von." I Fnid hastily. ••I &loam not ctream of repeating It, 110 Pr3teeted• "I—er---I merely propose to ex- plain it." "I alrl afraid my property is lost to me for ever," I said, more mildly; "but since you mean to try to reclaim it, I shall endeavour to forget all this u.nplec.cantness." "You are extremely kind, Miss—er -- Smith," he answered, as he moved aside to let me pass. Strange to say, hie success was magical, for my boxes arrived at the boarding-house in less than an hour. I wore my sweetest frock

In the Chancery Division on SalT?ay, hew.° Mr Justice Joyce, Mr. Liughe., K.C, srplied on behalf o Messrs Crosfleld, soap msnufacturere, of Warrington, for an injunction to prevent a former employee of the inpany from disclosing trade secreta. It no, an action upon motion for judgment in default of defence. The defendant, Fred, rick Wright, was at ono time in the plaintiffs' employ IT a workman in the oil treatment dei artment of their tusiness, and on the 27th of October, 199, he entered into an agrr erncnt of service with the firm fur a period of ten yea's, and, further, that he would not during that time, nor within two years afterwards, without the content in writing of the company, " disclose, divulge, or communicate " to any person any information vthateoever as to these subsiancra or articles with which he was conversant in their bueinr s I and in the manufacture of whl3h he bad been specially engaged. In April, 1912, Wright left the plaintiffs' employ and they alleged that he had offered to sell to cestain persons information concerning the secret pro- cess of the plaintiffs' roanu'ectures. He had also offered his services to assist in working them. Mr Hughes slid he asked for injunction for the period of the agreement and for the two years further. Ills Lordship said prima facie the plaintiffs were entitled to it, but in applying for the two years beyond be was going rather wide. Mr Hughes said he mu,t ask for the whole term. His Lordship granted the injunction asked fur.

HERO FUND.! CARNEGIE AWARD FOR EARLEcITOWN WIDOW. The Carnegie Hero Trust Fund, at their meeting at Dumfermline, decided to make an allowance of Mr. per week to Mrs. Eavea and her family, of Regent-street Earlcatown.

Mrs. Eavts is the widow of the man who, while eruployrd at the Viaduct Waggon Works, belonging to !be London and North. Western Railway Company, in June, gave his life io order to save that of an elderly men named Potts, weo was working with him. Eaves was crushed between the buffers of a war gun and kilied while in the act of pulling Potts out of the way of the buffers and saving his life. The award is subject to alteration and rev. cation, but It will continue to Mrs. Eaves as long as she remains a widow and the trustees are satitil d that the money is being properly used. Stretton. „" WALING DA.Y."—The children observed this ~"°Pular annual festival last week. A short service "S held in church in the afternoon, when an address given by the Rev W S Adams, of Deresbury. Sub- tly the children marched through the parish. ,ramme of races and other athletic events was in a field lent by Mr Mackshavv. Mr and Mrs were warmly welcomed to the gathering. Mrs gave several presents to children who had been -"ecessful in an exhibition of flowers. The Blue Coat 01 Band was in attendance. Winwick.

div.head: Moore.
div.p: Moore.

Cnorn Trat..—The Wesleyan Choir had their annual excursion on Wednesday. ibe train left Moore station for Rhyl at 6.25. The morning seemed to be rather favourable hut as the destination was being reached the clouds gathered and covered the sun, and he was never seen again through the whole of the day. The rain caused the choir members (and friends who accompanied them), to seek what amusements the town afforded under cover. Dinner and tea were partaken of at Hopwood's Cafe, High-street.

Lymm. PR/MITIVE METHODIST SERMONS.—The anniversary services of the Broom Edge Primitive Methodist Chapel were held on Sunday, when Mr James Bernard, elocu- tionist, of Altrincham, preached excellent, sermons at both the afternoon and evening services. ACCIDENT TO AN ERRAND BOY.—While cycling round the corner by Mrlinston's house, just past the station, on Saturday morning last, one of the errand boys employed by Mr W Tomlinson, confectioner, of the village, came into collision with a motor car and was thrown on to the road. He sustained a deep cut on the knee which was afterwards stitched up by the doctor. BULL AT THE BAR.—The proverbial story of the bull in the china shop had quite an amusing, if less destruc- tive, rival on Monday night when a bull which was being quietly taken through the village entered the door of the Spread Eagle Hotel and walked right up to the bar where, no doubt thinking its surroundings rather to strange, it turned round and slowly walked out into the street again. CONGREGATIONAL CHOIR TRIP.—The Congregational Choir went for their annual trip on Wednesday. The venue this year was Rhyl. Unfortunately they must have chosen the wrong day for heavy rain fell most of the time, spoiling any pleasure that would have been gained out of doors. However the members made the best of the day by visiting the various indoor enter- tainments that were held in the resort. PAnisH CHURCH EXCURSION.—The annual excursion of the Parish Church Sunday school was held on Thurs- day, when a large number of scholars and friends, accompanied by the Rector' paid a visit to Blackpool. The Tower, Big Wheel, and Fair Ground at South Shore afforded much amusement for the gayer excursionists, while the quieter members were able to have a happy time ou the shore, piers, and by inspecting the new promenade. SONS OF TFAIPERANCE.—On Saturday; the Lymm members of the Order of the Sons of Temperance enjoyed a very pleasant outing to Llangollen. The town and its famous old Gothic Bridge— one of the " Seven Wonders of \Vales," was thoroughly insgected. Many places of interest in the district were visited including Berwyn with its Horse Shoe Fails, Church, and Chain Bridge. Amongst other items of amusement a trip to Pontcyssylltan Aqueduct and back in a boat on the Toy Canal was indulged in. After a safe arrival home all expressed their pleasure at the enjoyable day's outing they had experienced on the banks of the sparkling Dee and amongst the bold Welsh hills. CHRISTIAN ENDEAVOUR —The Warrington Wycliffe and the Lymm Independent and Primitive Methodist Christian Endeavour Societies, together with the Lymm Congregational Christian Service Band, held a joint open-air meeting in the Rookery, Booth's Hill, on Monday evening. The meeting was opened by Mr A Thomas before a large assembly. Mr Beswick, of War- rington, gave an interesting and helpful address on the words "Come unto Me all ye that labour and are heavy laden and I will give you rest." He pointed out that the spiritual rest required from the daily turmoils of our life could only come by taking Christ into our hearts and homes. Mr R Hewitt, of Lymm,also spoke a few words, taking his theme from Noah and the Ark, showing how God had protected Noah end his family from being destroyed by the flood which was to drain the world of all wickedness, and bow God would save us if we would only take Him into our lives and meet with Him in His house Sunday by Sunday. The Rev W B Whiteway before closing said that the churches in Lymm were half empty on Sundays, and impressed upon parents the necessity of their attending some place of worship and of also sending their children. He con- cluded the meeting with a few words of prayer and the benediction. - -

ASSAULTED HIS COUSIN.—Lest week-end Booth's Hill was the scene of some disturbqnce. Soon after 11 o'clock on Saturday night as ,M r Thomas Henry Percival, of Newfield, Lymm' was proceeding along Baoth's Hill with a friend he passed his cousin, a younger man named Samuel Percival, t dking to another man, and thinking that he overheard a remark that referred to himself, he crossed over to Samuel Percival to ask for en explanation. For some reason, Samuel Percival, who was under tho influence of drink, struck his cousin over the eye with a pint bottle full of beer, causing a nasty cut which bled freely, and had afterwards to be stitched by Dr. Adams Acting-Sergeant Robinson coming on to the scene took Samuel Percival to the Police Station where be was remanded until Monday afternoon when he was charged before Messrs W P Rylsnds and W G Groves, with unlawfully wounding his cousin Thomas Henry Percival by striking him on the forehead with a bottle at Booth's Hill, Lymm, on Saturday night. After the hearing of the case the accused was fined Bs. 6d. costs, and bound over to keep the peace for twelve months. THE TERRITORIALS. On Sunday evening the Lymm detachment of the sth (Earl of Chesters's) Battalion Cheshire Regiment, about forty men in number, under the command of Lieutenant W C Hartley, entrained for Carnarvon where they are going under canvas for periods of seven to twenty one days. Many friends gathered on the plat- form to see the departure and a hearty " send off " was given. The camp this year will be of special interest to the Lymm men as the commander of the Cheshire Territorial Force is Major Groves of Dean's Green, Lymm. The Lymm detachment can now claim the distinction of being a half battalion their numbers having reached fifty men. Torrential rains fell during Sunday and Monday nights, and the Bethel-road camp, which is the head- quarters of the Cheshire Infantry Brigade,presented on Tuesday morning a storm-swept appearance. The low- lying portion of the ground was flooded, so much so in the case of the 3rd IA elsh Brigade Royal Itield Artillery that the quarters of officers, men, and horses had to be removed nigher up. The North Wales Infantry Brigade fared better at Coed Helen owing to the more . sheltered nature of the ground. General Sir Francis Lloyd visited both brigade on Tuesday, and inspected the lines briefly. An officer of the sth Cheshires had the misfortune to slip on the muddy ground, and sustained a somewhat serious injury to his leg.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
LORD WOLMER ALARMED.

Lord Wolmer, M..P.,addressed the Newton Division Conservative Association on Saturday afternoon, and said it would not be long before they put the Govern- ment into a rninority,and then the Unionist party would come into their own again. It was now becoming apparent that the Government, and especially Mr Lloyd George, were not very anxious io fight the next general election on their past record, either on Insurance or Welsh Disestablishment or Home Rule. The election would be fought on a set of new promises, and a new red herring in the guise of their old friend—the land policy. Ile (the speaker) had no doubt but that they should have the same old barrel organ on the market square playing that good old American tune, " The Land song." (Laughter). There was one subject upon which he hoped the battles of party warfare would not be fought, and that was the British Navy. It was apparent that the country was now in greater danger than it was when Napoleon and his army were ready to cross to Dover. The greatest navy they had ever seen was within a few hours' steam of our shores, end that was a risk which it would be criminal folly for any British statesman to ignore. Whatever Government was in office must take care to see that the British Navy was not only strong enough to meet and defeat any foreign force but strong enough with an abundant margin for all possible contingencies which fortune might bring. They bore no ill-will to the German people and they did not complain of their naval policy, but they silently resolved that that navy should never be sufficiently powerful to wipe out Eng- land's supremacy at sea, which was the only guarantee of England's national existence. (Applause.)
During the severe thunderstorm on Friday morning one of the Manchester liners, the Manchester Port, was driven ashore in the Mersey, but was got off again two hours later. A flat was also sunk.

Church Lads' Brigade. The Warrington battalion of the Church Lads' Brigade, or to give it its new title, the 2nd Liverpool Cadet Battalion C.L.8., had a church parade to the Parish Church OD Sunday evening. There V. as a muster of 160 officers. N.C.O.'s and lads who assembled on the open space near Arpley Cannons and proceeded to church, via Mersey-street. Lieut.-Colonel Appleton was in command, assisted by Major Brooks and Captain and Adjutant Sankey. The combined bugle bands of the St. Paul's and Stockton Heath companies were in attendance. The Rev Dr Figgis of the Community of the Resurrection, preached a powerful sermon on the need for self-denial as part of the discipline of the Christian. After the service he inspected the battalion which was lined up in Church-street. At the Arpley Cannons, before the companies were dismissed. Lieut.-Colonel Appleton said he was very proud of the parade that night, and the band, their playing reflecting great credit upon them. That was the last time be would address them before leaving for camp, but he hoped they would keep up the good name of the battalion. He bad never put a soldier on his honour who had not loyally responded, and now be put all those who were going in camp at Ripon upon their honour. He wished them all a happy time.

St. John's Presbyterian Church. The temptations to which we are appointed, was the topic of the Rev W Reid's discourse on Sunday evening at St John's. While God tempts not in the sense of soliciting to evil Be nevertheless leads men into temptation at appointed times for a definite purpose, viz. : that of determining and fixing character. The Lord Jesus Christ identified himself completely with humanity in the ordeals of baptism or dedication, and temptation unto fitness for service. The creation of man as a free agent means in every life opportunity. Opportunity has for its other side temptation. The prayer lead us not into temptation " just means "Prevent my vocation from becoming my temptation," or "Let me not put myself where I shall be triad over- much." After touching on the threefold temptation of Christ, to attempt life wholly on its lowest platform, to live for popularity, to achieve pre-eminence by compromise with evil, the preacher contrasted the man whose gifts directed to ends of wealth, reputation, &c. at last finds his life blasted, and his occupation his prison with the man who, losing himself, directs his gifts to service, tempted all along with self distrust, but in every temptation developing his power, entering into the joy of the victor afforded by angelic ministra- tions and sharing the throne of Christ.

div.head: Wycliffe Congregational Church.
div.p: Wycliffe Congregational Church.

The Rev. F. Chalmers Rogers, M.A., senior student of the Yorkshire United College and a grandson of the late Dr. J. Guiness Rogers, conducted the services at Wycliffe Congregational Church on Sunday. At the morning service he told a story to the children on "Going straight" and drew a useful lesson showing the importance of having Christ as a guide through life. The sermon was based on the incident in Simon's house, recorded in Luke vii., 34. He pointed out that sins of oommission condemned the world but sins of omission prevented the world from being saved. The measure of their love for Christ was according to the measure of their sense of indebtedness to Him. A self-righteous man did not feel his need of Christ. What we wanted, as Mr. Gladstone said, was not more sin, but more of the sense of sin. 'The evening discourse was based on the words of Pilate" What is truth ? " (John xviii., 38). Truth, he said, was the great problem of the ages. Ever since man was civilised his highest quest had always been the quest of truth that he might unlock the door of mystery Truth was the highest vision of what was right that dawned upon our sonl from one moment to another. The preacher proceeded to quote Christ's words " I am the way, the truth and the life," or in other words " I am the truth, therefore the way and the life." It was the duty of Christians to be true to the truth as Christ revealed it, for it was only as they strove to live up to Christ's ideal that they were true. The Rev John Davidson, of Newton-le-Willows, will preach morning and evening tomorrow (Sunday).

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.—Open Meeting.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.—Open Meeting.

There was a good attendance at this meeting on Sunday, presided over by Mr. George Wallingtop, who spoke upon several Biblical women, whose characters were examples to all woruen.—Mr. E. Wynne Jones gave the address upon "The Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of Man." He said that whet was needed in our day was a revival of the old social con- science as it was set forth in the Gospel, and cause it to permeate the life of the nation. We must re-atiirm, and that with no uncertain voice, the great principles of Christian brotherhood. It was quite clear that Christianity meant a great deal more to the early Church than it does to us to-day, and their nearness in point of time to the great founder Jesus Christ, placed them in the best position to understand the true significance of Christ's teaching. They believed that Christianty should influence life at every point. We heard a great deal to-day about industrial unrest and the social problem,these difficuties existed because men had wandered away from the teaching of Jesus Christ, and the only solution of our social problems was the practical application of the principles of Christian brotherhood. We had had during the last few days a Socialist leader praying that" God would strike Lord Devonport dead. The great bulk of Socialists abhore a thing like that. But if we only insisted on the principles of Christ being the ruling principle in State and Church. Lord Devonport and every other employer would have to do what was right to the worker. It was said that Christians were so much concerned with the world to come that they bad no time to think about the present one. Someone said to Moody, the evangelist, "My citizenship is in heaven "and Moody very rightly replied " Get it down here and strive to improve the present." I have read somewhere these words " The fact is preachers and congregations are bound hard and fast in a system that is materialistic and without a single noble aspiration. The average preacher and churchgoer does distinctly believe not only that it is right to eat without work- ing but to get fed, clothed, housed, insured and huried in the bargain." They ought to ask themselves, was there any ground for these changes ? Be was sure there would not beg only they proclaimed the Gospel in all its fullness and maintained the same proportions that our Master did. Jesus Christ had much to say about the world to come but he had a great deal more to say about the brotherly relations that should exist among men as a result of their belief in the Fatherhood of God. The Fatherhood of God carried with it and involved the brotherhood of men. it was the duty of every man to take an interest in these matters. Emerson tells us that " the power of love as the basis of a State has never yet been tried." What we wanted was that the principles of Jesus Christ should become the ruling power in all that affected our national life. He believed that we were entering on a new era, an era of effort after an organisation of the community which should secure more general well- being for all, and a wider diffusion of all that made for the welfare of humanity. We must educate, regulate, legislate, and help on the time when every man should have an equal opportunity of living the best life. • ' ST. HELENS.

div.head: GLASS TANK BURST.
div.p: GLASS TANK BURST.

Shortly after ele-ve-n-o'-ci-o-ck-oirltio-riday morning one of the large glass tanks at Messrs. Pilkington Bros'. sheet glass works at St. Helens burst and set the place on fire. The roof of the tankhouse was quickly alight. The molten glass ran in all directions among the surround- ing buildings and gave out a heat which made it diffi- cult for the firemen or anyone to approach the tank - house. Considerable difficulty was experienced in con- fining the glass to one place but the firemen and work- men, who have bad considerable experience in these matters, did all that was possible to prevent further damage. Some time will elapse before the tank can be rebuilt and put in order, but the men concerned will be employed in other parts of the work.

- A WIFE'S "INDISCRETION." COUNTY COURT SEQUEL TO PIANO SALE. At St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, Mr Goldie (instructed by Messrs Kelly and Picton) asked for jndgment on behalf of Robert 0. Tunstall, ot St. Helens, against Charles H Kelsall, a former manager of a St. Helens engineering works, and Zillah A Kelsall, his wife, for £l3, balance of account in respect of . a piano. On February 22 last, it was stated, the defendants purported to sell plaintiff a piano, for which Tunstall paid £lB. It was alleged that at the time of the sale Mrs Kelsall, with the knowledge and at the request and for the purposes of her husband, made fraudulent mis- representations and gave certain warranties as to the piano, which induced the plaintiff to purchase. The defendants had no title to sell the piano, and in the events which had happened plaintiff had been deprived of it. The defendants had paid .£l2, and judgment %as asked for £l3 balance. Judge Shand said there was a letter for the defendant from Victoria embankment, Darlington, which stated that Mrs Kelsall was too ill to travel, and asking for an adjournment. Kelsall offered to pay the £9 35 on Friday, and said the whole case was the outcome of a serious indiscretion on the part of his wife, of which he was not cognisant at the time. Mr Goldie said it was a very serious matter, and in the first case proceedings were contemplated in another court. He accepted judgment for the amount of £9, and his Honour gave an order for costs on scale A.

div.head: tALL RIGHT 9 ItESIRVED.]
div.p: tALL RIGHT 9 ItESIRVED.]
THE WRONG WOMAN
BY MRS. COULSON KERNAIIAN, Author of " Tho Bag Under tho Thatch, "House of Bin-mon," •' No Vindication," "An Unwiso Virgin." "Devastation," ite.
All tho way from London Bridge to Brighton llobert .Crayshaw was savagely wishing hie wife

would die. It was When the train was thundering thrdugh the tunnel which had been the scene of more than one tragedy that it occurred to Crayshaw that he might assist his wife out of the world. Some thoughts stamp themselves upon the countenance in spite of a man, nor is it °seenvial - that the eyes should be looked into that the thoughts should be road. Crayshaw was looking down at something which lay in the hollow of his hand as the train emerged from the tunnel, yet, an old woman' who sat directly opposite to him, and who chanced to look into his face, told a friend afterwards that his look gave her "quite a turn." The thing which Crayshaw held in his hand was a hypodermic syringe. It was for himself he had purchased it, together with a supply of morphia, which lay in his boast pocket. Re had for a long time been sleepless, for he had rashly speculated with his wife's money as well

itslifs oWn. He had just been to visit his father-in-law, whose health was fast failing, and he had not been well received. Old Mr. Liscombe was not noted for a particularly • good temper, even when his health was good. But since illness had attacked him, his fits of passion were such as to terrify. He had given Robert Crayshaw " bit of his mind "that afternoon; for that hand- some young man's foolhardy squandering of money was no secret. The piece of mind" was seasoned with so many unpleasant adjec- tives that Mildred Liscombe, the old man's niece, had been quite sem, for Robert, and had ' told him so in the dining-room, whither she had followed the young man after he had left ,the bed-chamber. "Ho is like that to everyone but me," Mil- dred had remarked, to chew Robert that the attack was more an ebullition of temper than real animus. But Mildred chewed Robert something else by her remark—something quite different. Ho saw that Mildred, and not his wife, would come into the old man's fortune. He had mar- ried Annie for the sole reason of coming into possession of her father's money. It was clear he had married the wrong woman. Robert Crayshaw was one of those men who, though utterly destitute of a single quality meriting regard, was undoubtedly attractive to the other sex; and he knew it, and worked it for all it was worth. Mildred was sorry for him; she had looked upon him with foolish, pitying eyes. He had but to exert his power of fascination to win her more entirely, and he know it. Oh, if Annie were only dead! He had had no particular animus against the little woman waiting for him in Russel-square, that is, until now. She had never stood in his light before. The train—the 5.5 express from London Bridge—steamed into Brighton Station. Robert Crayshaw gathered up his papers, and left the carriage while the train was still in motion. He would have come to grief had not! et little woman sprung forward, seizing his arm as he staggered on the edge of the platform so perilously near the moving train. "Oh, Bob!" gasped this man's preserver, 'Won't, don't ever do it again; you might lave been killed! " Robert Crayshaw could not look at his wife. He was unaccountably angry with her. Why had she come to the station? It made a man look such a fool to be met by his wife. And why had she put him under an obligation? This was the worst part of it. There were plenty of porters who could, and no doubt would, have come to his rescue. He took hold of her arm to hurry her along. His fingers pressed into her soft flesh till she winced. "Not so tight Bob dear," she said, as involuntary tears sprang to her blue eyes. He glanced at her, and noted the starting tears and the downward droop of the tremulous mouth. "For heaven's sake don't make a scene ! " he told her, in a tone which absolutely frightened her. " You should not have done what you did. You might have swung round and fallen be- tween the platform and the train." As he spoke these words the thoughts he had had in the tunnel came back to him. How 'easily it might have happened accidentally then! '

They had come to the barrier. Crayshaw gave up his ticket, and the two passed through the booking office across the station yard, and into Queen's-road. Then the ma's changed his tactics ." Forgive Trio, littlo woman," he said, in a voice which could be very tender when he chose, and ho chose now. "I was excited by nearly getting under that blank train." She glanced up at these words, gladly enough, but tears once more dimmed her eyes. Crayshaw wished she had not that detestable habit of be-

coming lachrymose at the least provocation. But be had made his plans, and complaioiiig with her now was no part of them. "How is my father?" she asked him, seeing that he had recovered his good humour, and feeling it safest not to further allude to his former ill-humour. "Breaking up fast, I fear," he told her. "And did you ask him if I might come to sco him?"
"-Yes; but he thinks a visit from you would excite him and make him worse. Now, don't be- gin to cry again! He may change his mind any, moment and wire for you:"

"Ilp Mildred with Min?". ,• es. He won't have anyone else near him." "I believe he cares more for Mildred than for his own daughter." She spoke resentfully. She had expressed his own thoughts, but he answered her as if, he con- sidered she had spoken foolishly. "What non- sense!" he said. "Sick people are always fanci- ful, He likes Mildred to wait on him and contri- bute to his comfort. That is natural enough. She has been his housekeeper since you married. I daresay he won't let you come to see him be- cause you shed tears on the least provocation. That sort of thing worries a man, you know." They had come to a corner, where a wall is al. ways covered with big advertisements. Be looked at one, and said, suddenly: "See! the Kendals are here to-night. It is 'The Ironmaster.' Would you like to go?" She was childishly delighted. "Of course should!" she cried. "Well, then, we will run in and tell Mrs. Biggs we shall not he in to dinner; and you can put on a pretty frock; and we will go and have some dinner out, and go to the play after." He was resolved to show himself on good terms with his wife before everyone. That was part of his plan too. There was something horribly cold-blooded about this handsome man, who had not yet reached thirty. Selfishness had always been the mainspring of Isis life. He was usually charming, because he found himself the gainer by' this atti- tude. His own comfort was the one thing that mattered. Money was essential to his com!ort. If he could get it and commit no evil, he prefer- red that. But if he could not, well, the evil had got to be done. The more he thought of the fortune old Liscornbe had accumulated, the more he craved it. Had he only foreseen that Mildred would worm herself into the old man's affections. he would certainly have married her instead of .Annie. Annie must be got rid of. He began to think it was really rather fine of him to make her last days pleasant, which he fully intended to do. Ho would spend freely on her out of the few hundreds which remained to him of tho money she had brought him on their marriage. Her father had asked him why he did not practice at the Bar. He had not said—as, he might have done—that he had not the smallest intention of practicing at the Bar, or of working at all, for the matter of that. He felt very ill- used that he should be taking rooms for his Brighton holiday, when that skinflint, his father- in-law, ought to have supplied means for him to stay at the Metropolo or the Grand. He wanted a good motor. He wanted to buy a likely filly he had heard of from a trainer at Lewes. He wanted to go with some friends to Assouan. What didn't he want? And Old Liscombe's money could do it all. It was clear to his legal mind that, in order to spite a detested son-in-law, these, coveted riches would be left to a niece—a niece, too, who could be had for the asking were he only a free man. Arriving at the boarding-house in Russell- square, where just now 40 one else was stay- ing, Crayshaw picked up a bundle of letters lion) the hall table, and opened them where ho stood, while his wife ran to her room to don a pretty frock. She was delighted at the thought of beirl taken out, for she had been left alone so much of late; and the thoughts that had been her companion had been very, very sad. She loved and admired her handsome husband, but she had come to realise that the love was only on one side. He did not care for her, and aornetirpes she had caught a look in his eyes very b-ko contempt. Of course, she was not worthw of him. She was small, and colourless, and insignificant, yet there was no task, no peril, she interests, would have shrunk from in hia T'''rlight she was glad. He had spoken to bar 0.4 itacCtioliate tclw. interest in what she would. wear. Perhaps he was beginning to Caro for her! She put on a frock of pearl grey and her er- mine stole and ha:6, and looked at herself criti- cally. Her joy had brought a pink tinge to her cheeirs. Her eyes looked bright. She was satis- fied, and flew downstairs, wishing not to keep her husband waiting. He was in the dining-room now, and was burning letters. He turned to her with a light laugh, which she would have found unnatural had she been less slow to see things. "How pretty you look!" he exclaimed; and the landlady, who was passing the door, over- heard the remark, which Crayshaw had in- intended she should. "I will run up and change," he added, "and then we will be off." One of the letters he had received had told him that he was on the brink of ruin--unless, yes, unless— Unconsciously, in the theatre that night his wife made his task seem easier. She irritated him beyond measure by weeping over the sor. rows of the heroine Claire. He noted, when the lights went up, that her complexion had suffered M the process. To his unsympathetic and critical mind she seemed hideous. But he shewed no sign. It wits when they got home that evening that he taught her the use of the hypodermic syringe. "Why not try it yourself?" he suggested when he had used it on his arm. "You don' sleep well, either." How easy, how terribly easy she was to aes. with! He almost hated her feebleness of charac- ter. He filled the syringe up to a certain mark, and gave it to her to press home herself. This was the beginning. They were in the dining-room alone when this occurred, and Crayshaw had rung the bell just as his wife bared her arm, and Mrs. Biggs entered as the air' was driving the needle home.

The landlady glanced' at this, to her, queer per- formance. but made no remark. Crayshaw asked to be called at seven o'clock, and Mrs. Biggs, after asking if they would require anything else, withdrew. Why do you want to be called so early?" asked Annie, glancing at the speck of blood upon her arm. "Are we not doing this to get a nice

long sleep?" He smiled a crooked smile. Her words to him sug;:-ested so much. A few more weeks, and the speaker would be taking—a nice long sleep! He told her that he had an engagement with a trainer at Lewes early in the morning, and he had ordered a trap, and they were to drive over together. It all sounded natural enough. Yet Crayshaw's motive for ringing the bell just when he did was not that he might ask to be called early. It would be very important in a few weeks' time to be able to produce a witness that his wife used a hypodermic syringe. It was February; but there was plenty of bright sunshine at Brighton, and every day Cray- thaw took his wife out on the sea front, pro- menading. up and down in the sight of everyone He bought her a black toy Pomeranian dog, which she decorated with ribbons, and adored. He was more attentive and affectionate than he had ever shewn himself in their brief married life. Annie Crayshaw was superlatively happy. Despite the unpleasant reception which Mr. Liscombe had given this briefless barrister, he continued to go up to London to call upon his father-in-law, whom he did not see, however. But he did see Mildred Loornbe, who con- sidered him a most forgiving and ill-used man, and tried by extra cordiality on her part to make up for what she considered her Uncle's brutality. On one of these excursions! to London, Cray- shaw procured an extra supply of morphia. His wife, at his suggestion, continued its use. But he always prepared the syringe for her, and the close he gave was very small. She saw him use it on himself, but was ignor. ant of the fact that now he only injected water in his own arm. He had two bottles exact l y alike in the box where he kept his hypodermic arrangements. One contained morphia, and the other ',ogler. When the time should be ripe, the syringe which Annie Crayshaw would use on herself would do its work. The time depended on how long old Lis- combe lasted out. Curious it would seem that old Liscombe shbuld leave his big fortune away from his own child just to spite his son-in-law. He might have left it to her, and so tied it up that her husband could not touch it, thought Crayshaw. But no, the old man was much too cute" for that! He know his daughter's weak nature; she would inevitably give to her husband what he could not legally take from her. Crayshaw thought over one utterance of his father-in law's in these days till the words burnt into his brain. "Don't you count on dead men's shoes," he had said. Those words could only bear one meaning to Crayshaw's logical mind. The money would be Mildred's. He was tied to tho wrong woman. Yet he did not fail to realise that whichever of the girls he had mar- ried, his wife would not have come into the fortune. As for Annie, her life was so insignifi- cant, she was puny in nature, that it could scarcely make a difference to her or to anyone else that her departure from scenes terrestial was anticipated by a few years. It is a fact that this man was in no way troubled by con- science. He even considered himself humane. He could not have given her physical pain in the passing. She would die so pleasantly, he told himself. What could be more desirable than to sleep to death? But for him she might live to contract some painful disease to die of! She sometimes worried him by wanting to go to see her father, and crying about him—of course, crying. Sho cried when "Shan," the toy pomeranian, got ill through over-eating, But Crayshaw shewed no ill-temper about his wife's little spasmodic floods of tears now. We can all of us put up with a grievance with some degree of patience when wo know it is not to last. It was about a fortnight after that journey from London Bridge to Brighton when he had first conceived of the diabolical plan of ridding himself of his wife, that the moment came for the actual carrying out of his fiendish design. He had been to London, and seen the sym-ya• thetic Mildred. More than this, he had seen 'Sir Roden Raulines, the physician who had just been called in in consultation for his father-in- law. Sir Roden Raulines told the young man that now the life of Mr. Liscombe might be counted by hours. He was comatose, and would cer- tainly never recover consciousness. Crayshaw journeyed home feeling that Mil- dred's sympathies would be redoubled when she heard of the loss he had sustained—of his wife. This sympathy woirld be easily worked upon, and in due time a warkner feeling would take its place. He took Annie to the theatre again that I night. havinr gladdened her heart by tellio2

her Hilt her tamer was better, ana would see her no t day! Next day! That was true enough he thought, if spirits did see each other in that afterwards. It was in their bedroom that night, and not downstairs as it had often been before, that frayshaw produced the little leather box which contained the two bottles and the syringe. Annie chatted gaily of going to see her father next day, as her husband prepared the syringe for himself. He always did this with his back towards her. He pressed the ne-edle home, answering her talk with a word now and again. Then, as he prepared the syringe again, his hand shook in spite of himself, and a strange buzzing came into his ears. But he accomplished his task, and handed the syringe to his wife, who was standing in her cambric nightdress ready for bed. He turned away as she took it, nor did he face round till he heard the rustle of the bed- clothes. ' Then he walked towards the bed, and scarcely knowing what he did hung his watch on the bed-poet. She nestled down among the pillows, saying: "We must soon leave this business off, mustn't I we? It can't be good." " Yes," he answered, "we won't use it again after to-night. Go to sleep, I shall read for a few minutes." He felt he could not enter that bed. He sat in an easy-chair, under an electric light, and tried to read, glancing every now and then to- wards the bed, to be met by his wife's open eyes. How long she was going to sleep! But he him- self was growing strangely drowsy. He slept before she did, but she thought him still reading, and at last fell asleep herself. ;She awoke with a start in the early dawn to ttnd the electric light still burning, and her hus- band still in his chair. But how pale he looked! She sprang from the bed and ran to him. Inexperienced as she was, she knew that he was dead. But what she never knew then, or at any time, was that he had mistaken the bottles. The water had been injected into his wife's arm, the poisonous dose into his own.

Mildred Liscombe bent over the poor little widow consolingly. "Don't cry any more, dear. It can do no good," she said. "Oh, but he was so good to me," Annie sobbed. "These last weeks were a real honey- moon. He did care for me, Milly." Of course, dear, but try not to brood. We will go away and aravel, and teach you to forget. You are a rich woman now." "Yes, I know. But oh! that Bob had lived to share the money with me! You see, father left it unconditionally. Oh, we should have been so happy!" "I always thought that my uncle's bark was worse than his bite," said Mildred. "Oh, but he never properly Robert," Annie made answer.

THE TERRITORIALS.
Annual Camp Begins To-morrow.

The local Territorials—the 4th Battalion Prince of Wales's Volunteers(South Lancashire Regiment)—will enter upon their annual fortnight's training under canvas to-morrow (Sunday): The place chosen for the encampment is Kirkham, near Blackpool. The fatigue party, consisting of about 30 men, under the direction of Lieutenant and Quartermaster Ingram, left Warrington on Thursday morning and will have the camp in readiness for the arrival of the main body. The battalion will parade to-morrow (Sunday) at 12.15 noon and trains will leave Bank Quay Station at 1.25 and 1.40, the latter stopping at Newton-le- Willows to pick up the local company.

div.head: ANNUAL CHURCH PARADE.
div.p: ANNUAL CHURCH PARADE.

As has been the custom for many years on the Sunday preceding departure for camp, the battalion attended divine service at St. Paul's Church on Sunday morning. Notwithstanding the miserable weather conditions, there was a good muster, under the command of Lieut.-Colonel B Fairclongh. The men, headed by the band and drums, left the Drill Hall shortly after ten o'clock and marched to the church by way of Sankey-street, Horsemarket-street and Bewsey-street. The service was conducted by the Rev. W. Bracecamp (vicar of the parish and chaplain of the corps), and the Rev. E. E. Peters. The hymns sung were Onward, Christian soldiers," "All people that on earth do dwell," "Fight the good fight ' and "Rock of ages," the accompaniments for three of them being provided by the regimental band. Mr. Ernest Wilkes was at the organ. The Rev W Bracecamp, in the course of his sermon,. emphasised the importance of prayer, Bible reading and Sunday observance. Next he addressed himself parti- cularly to the question of national defence. "We are on the eve of a great crises—one without a parallel within the past 100 years—and our national forces are, unfit to meet the strain that may be put upon us with any assurance of success. Our position was never more- precarious than at the present time." Those were the words of a man who knew what he was writing about, as he was an old soldier and an expert who kept his eyes open. That old soldier told them they were in danger of being shipwrecked as a nation, and if he (the preacher) might use the illustration, they were in great danger of not being able to hold their own, when troubles came. What were the" helps "they were using? Thank 3od they had the Territorial system, which was something and which, generally speaking, had been a success. It appeared from the. returns which had been sent in from the various counties, that the regiments which had been formed up. and down the country were nearly up to the required strength, and the best part about the Territorial system was that they were having a better class of men. They were not piling loafers, but lads who loved their country and realized the importance of joining a regiment for their country's sake. The words he had quoted were the words of a soldier who had his head screwed on in the right way and who did not talk merely for the sake of talking, and it therefore behoved all civilians who bad not realized the importance of the statement he had read to do all they could for their country. The time was coming for compulsory service unless England woke up. He- did not believe it would be a bad thing for it, because there were many lads who liked, on a aay like that, to follow a regiment marching to and from church,because , they were delighted to applaud the soldiers, but were unwilling to join themselves and undergo the requisite training, because they lacked ern rgy. If they wished , to be at peace they must be prepared for war, and the only way to be prepared was for every eligible man, for , the sake of his country, to go into training and make himself an efficient soldier.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. HENRY FAIRCLOUGH.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. HENRY FAIRCLOUGH.

One of the most prominent aud respected figures in Lancashire commercial circles pa-sed away on Sunday. in the person of Mr. Henry Fain:lough, 37, Wilson Patten-street, Warrington. For a considerable time Mr. Fa irclough's health had been far from robust. Our readers will recall that Mr. and Mrs. Faircicugh met with a serious accident about two years ago when motoring along the Liverpool road at Bold. They eacountered a motor cyclist at a daogerous corner and in endeavouring tb avoid a eOlllBlOll the ear was turned into a wall. Mr. Fairclough was pinned beneath the car mid his ribs were fractured. A fortnight after the accident Mrs Fairclough died. To her hnaband her death was a great blow, from which he never frilly recovered, and his health seemed to decline from - that time. Mr. Fairclough was born at Earlestown on December 28th, 1849. He was the youngest son of the late Mr. James Fairciough, who established the' firm of Messrs. J. Faiiclough and Sons, Ltd., corn millers, Warrington. His education was received chiefly at the Boteler Grammar school, of which the late Mr: Cary was then the headmaster, and he began his business life with Mr. Brewis, cotton manufacturer, Golborne. Altering his original intention of entering the cotton'trade, he proceeded to Liverpool, where for a number of years lie was engaged wiih the firm of -Messrs. George McFarland and Co., corn merchants. On the retirement of his father he became a partner in the Mersey Mills firua. Ile continued in that capacity until the firm was made a limited compat v. From that time be acted as a managing director. Byl its enteprise the firm built up tor itself a great reputation and is now one of the leading concerns ia &nth West Lancashire. Messrs. Fairclough were the first to navigate the Meisey—ou the banks of which their mills stand—by steam. The telephone was first introduced into Warrivaton by them, and they were the first to order the automatic roller miller in Great Britain. -

The late Mr. Fairclough might justly have been 'described as one of the captains of the Lancashire coal industry. His associatkn with the CtAlins Green Colliery Co. Ltd., of which he WRS chairman and managing director, dated front 1872 His fellow- coal-owners paid a tribute to his sterling business qualities by electing him president cf the South-West Lancashire Association, which be also represented on the River Mersey Commission, lie was also a member of the Local Conciliation Board. After the rrcent coal strike Mr. Fairelcugh was elected a member of the Lancashire and Cheshire District Board, the first appointed under the Coal Mines (Minimum Wage) Act, but ill-health caused his resignation twu months

ago. Mr. Fairclough was held in high reepect in commeicial circles throughout the North of England, and those who were privileged to enjoy his friendship appreciated the kindliness, candour and geniality which, to those who did not know him intimately, might have seemed to be somewhat obscured by a natural brusqueness and reserve. Be was one of the staunchest and tiuest of friends, whose word was his bond and could always Le relied upon. In politics Mr. Fairclough was a Conservative, although he never actively interested himself in party warfare. Ile was also a strong Chutchman. In his leisure moments Mr. Fairclough took a keen delight in spurt, and many years ago was one of the best known cricketera in the district. He captained the town club when matches were played against the leading combinations in Lancashire, and the Warring- ton eleven at that period included *uz.,,h well-known players as the late Mr S M Crosfield, Mr J J Crosfield, Captain Manson, the brothers Lawton, T Aran-trong, the late Tom Jolley, Mr W H Podmore and Mr Clarke with Harry Tinsley and Fleetwood as pro- fessionals. The last match in which the deceased

gentleman played for the Arpley Club was at Bolton, on Jane 22nd, 1899, when Jerry Ellis bowled him for a "duck." Mr Faitclough was for many years on the Executive Committee of the Lancashire County and his wise judgment in the management of affairs at Old • Trafford was generally recognised. In more recent years Mr. Fsirclough had devoted himself with great enthusiasm to golf, and to the time of his death held the cartaincy of the Warrington Golf Club. The late Mr Fairclough married Miss Margaret Longton, daughter of the late Mr Peter Longtou, of Crouton. Theie were no children. THE FUNERAL.

Impressive scenes were witnessed at the funeral which took place at the Warrington Cemetery on Wednesday, the large and representative attendance constituting a striking tribute to the respect enter- tained for the deceased gentleman. The first part of thel service was held in Holy Trinity Church, the olliciating clergy heing :—The Revs E C E Carleton (vicar), H R Wild (curate) and 0 C Briggs (vicar of Christ Church, Latchford). The choir was in attend• ance and the hymns " My God ray Father, while I stray ' and " Now the labourer's task is o'er " were sang. Mr W B Randall was at the organ end as the col:in was borne out of the church he played" 0 rest

in the Lord " (Mendelssohn). The sun shone yesterday on the completion of 811 enterprise which is destined to prove gle.t boot, t.il some of the most thickly-populated per ti of lit an ing- ton. Under the happiest auspices, the Mayor (Coo, cillor Dr. J('seph) performed the ceremony LE opening the new footbridge which has been eri eted ecr o-a the Mersey to connect Howley and Latchford wade and afford more convenient access to Victot lark • heti la.s hitherto been possible to those living otr t-ir Lamm shire side of the river. The occasion was a mersorable one for dwellers in the !realities to he served by the bridge and large crowds assembled on the riaer leieks to witness the inauguration of this much-1A.00,1 anear,A of communication. The strueture is one of It tir. Ii a patent steel wire rope suspension bridges, e ith i clear span of 175 feet between abutments Oa ebtler semi: there ate two steel lattice pillars over which the suspension ropes pass. The ropes are of special high, tension galvanised steel w;re, specially splayed to give rigidity to the bridge. To the wires are fastened steel suspension rods, carrying girders to take the bridge flooring, which is of two itch timber planks. The clear width of the bridg is six feet. On tire Latchford side there are two embankments running froth the bridge, parallel to the river, one east and the other west, to give access to the different portions of vieo,ia Park. It is intended eventually to provide a public footpath along the river bauk from the bridge to Knutsfrrd-road which will remain open throughout the day and night. This provision will be especially welcomed by workingmen who have to be at their work in the early hours of the morning. The ceremony was favoured with bright weather and the lines of streamers with which the new bridge as decorated gave a festal touch to the scene. Members of the Town Council and Education Corn-1 mittee and other prominent townspeople gathered on the Howliy side of the bridge where the Mayor was formally to neclare the etructur e open. Among those present were tire Mayor and Msyoress. Alderman A Bennett, W Pierpoiut, J Smethurst, James Evans. John Evans, Councillors T Dirties, G Archer, J Skelland, C Jackson Holmee, T Chautler, W H J Jenkins, J Pemberton, J Dickiason, t' Lindley, T S W H Belden, E Cnnuington, J Sankey arid J , Halliwell, Messrs J tLyon Whittle (town clerk). Arnold Nield, E A White, A Perris. G May- bury, C I) Parkinson, Reginald Joseph, Cecil Joseph W Clegg and numerous ladies. Aldermen SMETHURST (chairman of the Bridge, Committee) said he had to perform the pleasant duty of asking the Mayor to declare the bridge open. The Itartet said he had taken part in mane cere- monies during his term of office, but none had: given him au much pleasure and satisfaction as that one, conferring, as it did, a great boon upon every inhabitant of the town, and more especially upon the dwellers in the wards immediately dencerned. Eta Wortsnir then drew aside the cord which had barred the spproach to the bridge and formally declared the footway and bridge open to the public, the crowd raising a hearty cheer. The Mayor and Mayoress then headed a procession across the bridge. On arriving at the Old Warps,the company took up positions on the Terrace, where more speeches were delivered. Alderman Smsmturisi proposed a vote of thanks to the Mayor for having opened that beautiful bridge." They were deeply indebted to him for the many kind- nessi s lie had extendtd to them during his term oF office. They were delighted to see the, bridge open and to know that after all their difficulties and trials. their perseverance had been crowned with success. (Applause). No more pleasing duty culd have fallen to the Mayor during his period of office than to open a bridge whish wc.uld give aceess to the park to so many thousands of children. (Applause). Alderman PIERPOINT seconded. div.head: 'ublic Rights and Speed Mania.
div.p: 'ublic Rights and Speed Mania.

Sir,—Lord Mersey's judgment on t'he loss of the Titantic will be gratifying to all who believe in sober and steady progress with a conscientious regard for public safety and public rights rather than the callous and mercenary ideas which have been making head- way on both sides of the Atlantic for about a quarter of a century. Considering the enormous loss of his. Lord Afersey might have been much more condemna- tory without being unjust, but it is satisfactory that he had no doubt about the calamity being due to excessive speed. Every unbiassrid person will agree with him and it remains now for the public to back up Lord Mersey and insist upon very drastic al orations. There is more thought for dividends an for humAn .life. That is the greatest evil of the present day. And if the • working classes are wise they will condemn and check the speed mania in all its fornip, as it simply means more com- petition and tarre sweating. It will not increase wages by a farthing in the long run. Fortunately railway companies have found that public con- fidence is a much more valuable asset than speed ecords, and as a c msequenee railway carriages are MAC th.e safest places in the world. The worst and incrA danger,ue form of speed mania is that which affects a certain class of motorists who seem to be mider the delurion that speed indicates brains, and win are allowed by the authorities to terrorise pedes- trians arid ignore rublic rights in a manner which hirridreds ot years ago would have caused riots in a week. Let us have some intellectual and social 'speeding up" by all means, hut this mechanical speed mania will not improve the condition of the manses in the smaileat degree.—Yours
W. CHRIMES.
