div.head: Teachers and Clerks—A Comparison.
div.p: Teachers and Clerks—A Comparison.

Sir,—l verm•ed with interest the letter which appeared in your issue of Saturday last under the beading of ''llw scai city of teachers." Your correspotideet, although he signs himself as " Ode who knows," displays his ignorance regarding the clerical prileseien when he states that "£145 is not the wages of a decent clerk who has never worried his head about any esiminations." The clerk's life is not a bed of roses, as painted by your correspondent, and when be refers to clerks !getting .£145 without having had any worry Ac., he is referring to the clerk of 30 }ears ago and not of the present day. If a clerk wishes to get anything like this figure he has got ta study and pass examinations in languages, book-keep- ing, &c. Does he consider his remarks applicable ,to advertisements rogarding situations such as the following—(thousands of which can be seen in the advertiet men t columns of the daily papers— :"German or Swiss Clerk wanted; under 26 ; must be good book-keeper, and able to speak and write English, French and German fluently. One with a slight knowledge of salesmanship preferred. Salary to com- mence 30. " "German, French, Shorthand, Corres- pondent, Book-keeper, commencing 255. Preference given to ono with a knowledge of glass trade and shipping." The above are Aennine advertisements ; and there is no doubt the advertisers would get hundreds of appli- cations, the same 'as a Manchester employer who advertised a few months ago for a clerk, and received 360 replies. One applicant who was educated at a orkshire College and afterwards at a University, asked for considerably less than .145 par annum—in fact there vas not one of the 360 applicants asked for anything like 5:145. There are clerks and clerks but a clerk to be a clerk burns more of the midnight oil than a teacher, because be is not blessed with long vacations and is not fortunate enough to leave promptly on the stroke of time, as he can very often be found working long after closing time. A teacher has about six or seven years studying, but a clerk's studies are never -finished, and when he has improved himself by studying he is not in the same fortunate position as the teacher, stare of a maximum of £145, because in the commercial world nowadays influence has taken the place of merit and abi:ity. I would advise " Oue who knows" to obtain a little more information regarding clerical life before he makes further misleadifig statements.—Yours HON olt ARY SECRETARY, Warrington Branch National Union of Clerks. 33, Orford-road, Warrington, July'29th, 1912.

div.head: Votes for Women. Window smashing and Hatchet throwing.
div.p: Votes for Women. Window smashing and Hatchet throwing.

Sir,—We have of late had evidences from those whom we look upon as representing high types of humanity which reveal that in the back gronad of their character there are savage instincts, or at 'any rate a belief in savage methods, It is surprising that the physical force policy is reverted to by a number, whose nature is cultivated and who, one w :old have thought, would hays been disciplined in self-restraint. Is is not strange that large numbers of intelligent, well educated, and well behaved women have lost faith in the power of truth and justice to win their causes, and have considered it necessary to 'unite physical force with these because they deem them alone not sufficiently powerful? When physical force is appealed to to hack up moral force, it reveals a loss of faith in the latter. " Might until Right is ready " seems to be the new motto. They must have the ally of violence to stiffen what they deem to be a just cause. They must have the double standard and the double force. As someone has well expressed it, they believe in force as a midwife to reform needed to bring the fruit of reason and of justice to the birth. The gravest danger of this alloy of force and right is that it involves a paid l ysis of the moral sense. An able writer in the "Nation" points this out. He says 'There comes a time when the violent mind closes automatic- ally before any questioning of the efficacy of its policy." The appeals made by the advocates of reason are addressed to deaf ears, and their adhei ents are only made more fanatical by them. They deem these appeals to be dictated by fear or treachery, and it seems to I stimulate them to fresh deeds of anarchy. These deeds of violence are seriously handicapping the pro- gress of the movement. First they turn against the movement timid supporters who have not a firm grip of the fundamental righteousness of the claim of women as human beings to the vote. Second, instead of creating fear, they strengthen the natural fighting instincts of all who oppose the movement. Third, they provide opponents with the powerful argument that the cauFe is not strong enough to win its way by reason, and hence force mu3t be called in to aid it. Thus a vitality is given to the opposing forces which has been grasped with avidity, all the more so, because the opposition has been so weak in reason. Fourth, it has had the effect of turning the thought of the people horn the rights of the question to such matters as the attempt at firing public buildings, window smashing, and hatchet throwing. Thus the movement has been dragged from its tJedestal where it fearlessly challenges reason, and been trailed in the mire and made ridiculous. t _ _

Should suffragettes read the above I doubt not in the curious working of their minds they will class me as an opponent of the cause, or as a false friend. May I make it clear that much as I deplore the appeal to force, which in my opinion is the most serious obstacle in the path of the enfranchisement of women. I have undiminished faith in the ultimate triumph of the cause, and while the follies of some may delay this triumph they cannot permanently rob women of what I deem to be their right and the State of their much needed full co-operation. If this be -so, what is the right direction in which the energies of tit, se who believe in female suffrage should be directed? Should not the point of concen- tration and the direction of effort be to convince the people, both men and women, t hat the step is a right one and therefore a wise one, that votes should be given to women as a right, and in view of the important duties and obligations to the 6tate which this right carries with it—in a word, to create an earnest public opinion? Granted that there are none more earnest for any reform than those who work for the suffrage, but the fact must be acknowledged that these so far—l mean those who are really earnest— are in the minority, and until they can be turned into a majority there is no hope for the movement. The window smashers will turn away in impatience from the emphasis we give to this necessity. Instead of creating an earnest public opinion they will return to their violent methods. Instead of convincing the people by reason they will go on trying, not to con- vince, but to frighten Cabinet Ministers by foolish and dangerous tricks. But the way I have indicated

Porter got comfortably settled, and his 32 stand included some really fine hits. It was indeed a credit- able not out performance. EiPoster ran up a score of 24 before he was caught by Craddock i row Hodgson's delivery. T Whitfield contributed a trio of runs, and after a not out score of 11 by Dickenson, the visitors declared with 77 runs. The Orford batsmen could not deal with the deadly bowling of their opponents the highest score being one of 11 from the bat of D Hewitt. The total was only one of 26 runs and the Sankey men look like retaining the premier position in the league. The Wilderspool team failed to put in an appearance on the Conservative Club ground and the matter will probably come before the League Committee at their next meeting. In the Warrington and District Sunday School League Walton Juniors entertained Stockton Heath at Walton but the visitors had little difficulty in winning by three wickets and fifty runs. Walker took practically all the wickets for the villagers and found the wet pitch very much in his favour. When be came to wield the willow be gave a very good account of himself and knocked up 28 runs before he was caught and bowled by Dutton The other seven players on the Stockton Heath side played well for the total score of 78. In a friendly encounter the St. Helens Cable Co. Juniors had a narrow win of one run over the ailborne- street B•ptists second team on the Arpley ground. 11;‘,,r the Cable team Mather bowled well, taking six wickets,

ANGLING. WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ANGLING A SSOCI ATION. (N.A. CENTRE). Mott of the Northern Anglers of Warrington were out for the opening match last week end, hut there are anglers who do not take part in contests. They prefer to go in for specimen fish and all the inducements that societies can place before them will not entice them from their particular sport. ImICKLE TRAFFORD. The Gowy was visited by a few members but no returns in the shape of coarse fish has been registered. The eels were fairly in the run. We have heird of one over Sibs having been taken. About 401h5 were sent from Ince way to Warrington on Tuesday last. They were taken in one night and a catch like this pays for several disappointments that the anglers have experi- enced these last few weeks. NORTON. Thecanal was fished by several members on Saturday, Sunday and Moucley, and sport was indulged in to a great extent but the roach by E Brookes still holds good for the July prize. A couple of members who were on holiday fished the canal Runcorn was and had a good weekend returning with about 101bs of good roach ranging from 3oz. up to (-1 and 7 ozs. CHESTER. We have had no report trom Chester but several members intend spending the week-end there. They are going to the Dee in the early hours of the morning and late in the evening. During the middle part of the day they will fish the canal—at least this is the pro- gramme they have mapped out ad they can be relied on to carry it out. LONG BARN. The flash here was visited by one or two members who reside in that district and we hear they hod one or two nice roach from the water. The carp and perch are rather backward here this season.
